approaches.idea: A value stack stores real elements while a parallel minimum stack stores the running minimum after each push. Both pop together so the min stack top is always the current minimum.
approaches.python:
class MinStack:
    def __init__(self):
        self.values = []
        self.minimums = []

    def push(self, value):
        self.values.append(value)
        current_min = value if not self.minimums else min(value, self.minimums[-1])
        self.minimums.append(current_min)

    def pop(self):
        self.values.pop()
        self.minimums.pop()

    def top(self):
        return self.values[-1]

    def get_min(self):
        return self.minimums[-1]


stack = MinStack()
stack.push(-2)
stack.push(0)
stack.push(-3)
results = [stack.get_min()]
stack.pop()
results.append(stack.top())
results.append(stack.get_min())
print(results)

approaches.name: Single Stack of Pairs
approaches.idea: Store (value, current-minimum) pairs on one stack. Every push carries the minimum of the new value and the previous pair's min, so one stack is enough and pop is a single operation.
approaches.python:
class MinStack:
    def __init__(self):
        self.stack = []

    def push(self, value):
        current_min = value if not self.stack else min(value, self.stack[-1][1])
        self.stack.append((value, current_min))

    def pop(self):
        self.stack.pop()

    def top(self):
        return self.stack[-1][0]

    def get_min(self):
        return self.stack[-1][1]


stack = MinStack()
stack.push(-2)
stack.push(0)
stack.push(-3)
results = [stack.get_min()]
stack.pop()
results.append(stack.top())
results.append(stack.get_min())
print(results)

approaches.name: Encoded Constant Space Stack
approaches.idea: When a new value would lower the minimum, store a code 2*value - oldMin instead and update the min. The code is always below the min, so both pop and top can detect it and reconstruct the previous minimum.

animation.hint: Each push records a minimum that can only ever shrink as values arrive.

approaches.name: Two Heaps
approaches.idea: Keep the smaller half in a max-heap and the larger half in a min-heap, rebalancing so their sizes differ by at most one. The median is the max-heap root, or the average of both roots when sizes match.

approaches.name: Sorted List with Binary Insertion
approaches.idea: Insert each new value into an always-sorted list at the index found by binary search, shifting the tail right. The median is read straight from the two middle slots.

approaches.name: Frequency Buckets
approaches.idea: Exploit the bounded value range by counting occurrences in a fixed array. To find the median, walk the cumulative counts until the middle rank is reached; additions are constant time.

animation.hint: Every new value passes through both heaps so the middle of the data stays balanced.

approaches.name: Sort and Compare
approaches.idea: An anagram is just a reordering, so two strings are anagrams exactly when their sorted character sequences are identical. Sorting loses the original order but trivially exposes equality.

approaches.name: Character Frequency Array
approaches.idea: Tally each letter of the first string in a 26-slot counter, then subtract each letter of the second. Equal character distributions leave the counter fully zeroed.

approaches.name: Prime Product Signature
approaches.idea: Assign each letter a distinct prime and multiply the primes of each string's letters. By unique prime factorization the two products match if and only if the letter multisets are identical.

animation.hint: Each character from s adds to the tally while the matching one from t subtracts it back down.

approaches.name: Backtracking with Start Index
approaches.idea: Run a depth-first search over candidate indices. At each level pick one candidate, subtract it from the remaining target, and recurse from the same index so the same number can be reused. When the remaining sum hits zero, a complete combination is recorded, and the path is unwound (backtracked) before trying the next candidate.

approaches.name: Dynamic Programming (Unbounded Knapsack)
approaches.idea: Build a DP table where dp[t] holds every combination that sums to t. For each candidate c, iterate targets t from c up to target and extend every combination stored at dp[t - c] by appending c. Because the loop over candidates is outermost, each number is used an unlimited number of times and every combination appears exactly once.

approaches.name: Include-or-Skip Recursion
approaches.idea: Walk the candidate array one element at a time and at each position make a binary choice: either take the current candidate (staying on the same index to allow repeats) or skip it and move on. When the remaining sum is zero a valid combination is saved, and recursion stops once every index has been decided.

animation.hint: Pick each candidate from the current start index, subtract it from the target, and backtrack when the sum is reached or exceeded.

approaches.name: Full 2D DP Table
approaches.idea: Fill an (m+1) by (n+1) table where dp[i][j] is the minimum number of edits to convert the first i characters of word1 into the first j characters of word2. Matching characters copy the diagonal value; otherwise the cost is 1 plus the best of insert, delete, or replace. The answer is dp[m][n] in the bottom-right corner.

approaches.name: Rolling 1D DP Array
approaches.idea: Each row of the DP table only depends on the previous row and the current cell to its left, so keep a single previous-row array and derive the next row into a fresh array, then swap. This preserves the exact same recurrence while cutting memory from quadratic to linear.

approaches.name: Memoized Recursion
approaches.idea: Define rec(i, j) returning the minimum edits for the suffixes starting at i and j. The recursion tries insert, delete, and replace (or advances both pointers when characters match), and a memo cache prevents recomputation of already-visited states. It is the top-down twin of the table-filling approach.

animation.hint: Fill dp[i][j] with the minimum edits for word1[:i] -> word2[:j], matching the diagonal or adding one operation.

approaches.name: Monotonic Decreasing Stack
approaches.idea: Sweep the temperatures left to right while maintaining a stack of indices whose temperatures are strictly decreasing. When the current temperature is warmer than the temperature at the stack top, pop that index and record the day distance as its answer. Each index is pushed and popped at most once, giving linear time.
approaches.python:
def daily_temperatures_stack(temperatures):
    n = len(temperatures)
    res = [0] * n
    stack = []
    for i, t in enumerate(temperatures):
        while stack and temperatures[stack[-1]] < t:
            idx = stack.pop()
            res[idx] = i - idx
        stack.append(i)
    return res


print(daily_temperatures_stack([73, 74, 75, 71, 69, 72, 76, 73]))

approaches.name: Right-to-Left with Answer Jumps
approaches.idea: Scan the array from right to left. For position i, start at i + 1 and follow the already-computed answer array: if the day at j is not warmer, jump j forward by res[j] days to its own next warmer day. A res[j] of zero means no warmer day exists ahead, so i has none either. No extra stack is needed.

approaches.name: Temperature Bucket Scan
approaches.idea: Temperatures are bounded (30..100), so keep an array next_w where next_w[t] stores the most recent index seen for temperature t. Walking right to left, the next warmer day is the smallest index among all buckets hotter than the current temperature. This trades the stack for a fixed-size bucket table.

animation.hint: Push each index onto a decreasing-temperature stack and pop days the moment a warmer temperature arrives.

approaches.name: Two-Pointer In-Place Compression
approaches.idea: Use one pointer (read) to scan consecutive equal characters and another (write) to place the compressed output back into the array. For each run the character is written first, then the digit characters of the run length if it exceeds one. The final value of the write pointer is the new array length.
approaches.python:
def compress(chars):
    write = 0
    read = 0
    n = len(chars)
    while read < n:
        ch = chars[read]
        count = 0
        while read < n and chars[read] == ch:
            read += 1
            count += 1
        chars[write] = ch
        write += 1
        if count > 1:
            for digit in str(count):
                chars[write] = digit
                write += 1
    return write


chars = list("aabbccc")
length = compress(chars)
print(length, chars[:length])

approaches.name: Recursive Run Compression
approaches.idea: Compress the array by processing one run of identical characters per recursive call. Each call finds the end of the current run, writes the character and its digit length at the write position, then recurses on the remaining suffix. The base case returns the final write index once the array is exhausted.

approaches.name: Build-Then-Copy (Stream)
approaches.idea: First assemble the compressed string in a separate buffer by streaming runs of equal characters and appending each character plus its digit length. Then copy the assembled string back over the head of the original array. This cleanly separates the run-detection logic from the in-place writing requirement.

animation.hint: A read pointer scans each run while a write pointer places the char and its digit count, advancing only on writes.

approaches.name: Iterative Group Reversal
approaches.idea: Count the list length first so only complete groups are reversed. A dummy node guards the head, and for each group of k nodes the nodes after the group's tail are repeatedly plucked and inserted right after the group's boundary, reversing them one node at a time. After a group is reversed the boundary advances to the group's new tail and the process repeats.
approaches.python:
class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = next


def build_list(values):
    dummy = ListNode(0)
    tail = dummy
    for v in values:
        tail.next = ListNode(v)
        tail = tail.next
    return dummy.next


def to_list(head):
    vals = []
    while head:
        vals.append(head.val)
        head = head.next
    return vals


def reverse_k_group(head, k):
    length = 0
    node = head
    while node:
        length += 1
        node = node.next

    dummy = ListNode(0, head)
    prev = dummy
    while length >= k:
        cur = prev.next
        for _ in range(k - 1):
            nxt = cur.next
            cur.next = nxt.next
            nxt.next = prev.next
            prev.next = nxt
        prev = cur
        length -= k
    return dummy.next


print(to_list(reverse_k_group(build_list([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]), 2)))

approaches.name: Recursive Group Reversal
approaches.idea: Advance k nodes ahead to verify a full group exists; if fewer than k nodes remain, return the list untouched. Otherwise reverse the first k links with a standard pointer flip, then attach the old head (now the group's tail) to the recursive result of the remaining suffix. The recursion hands back the new group head at every level.
approaches.python:
class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = next


def build_list(values):
    dummy = ListNode(0)
    tail = dummy
    for v in values:
        tail.next = ListNode(v)
        tail = tail.next
    return dummy.next


def to_list(head):
    vals = []
    while head:
        vals.append(head.val)
        head = head.next
    return vals


def reverse_k_group_rec(head, k):
    cur = head
    count = 0
    while cur and count < k:
        cur = cur.next
        count += 1
    if count < k:
        return head
    new_tail = head
    prev = None
    cur = head
    for _ in range(k):
        nxt = cur.next
        cur.next = prev
        prev = cur
        cur = nxt
    new_tail.next = reverse_k_group_rec(cur, k)
    return prev


print(to_list(reverse_k_group_rec(build_list([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]), 2)))

approaches.name: Array Chunk Reversal
approaches.idea: Linearize the linked list into a plain array of values, then reverse each block of k values independently while leaving a trailing partial block untouched. Rebuild a brand new linked list from the transformed values. This is the simplest to reason about at the cost of extra linear memory.

animation.hint: For each group, repeatedly move the node after cur to right after prev, then step prev to the group's new tail.

approaches.name: Top-Down DP with Memoization
approaches.idea: Recursively match the input and pattern from positions (i, j). A dot matches any single character, while a star applies to the preceding token and matches either zero of it (skip two pattern chars) or one more of it (advance i, keep j). Results for each (i, j) state are cached so the exponential recursion becomes polynomial.

approaches.name: Bottom-Up 2D DP
approaches.idea: Fill a boolean table dp[i][j] meaning s[:i] matches p[:j]. The first row is initialized by consuming pattern stars that cancel their preceding character. Each subsequent cell either copies the diagonal when characters align, or combines the zero-match and repeat-match options for a star. The answer is dp[m][n].

approaches.name: Rolling 1D DP
approaches.idea: Each table row depends only on the row above and the current row's earlier cells, so the whole DP can be evaluated with a single previous-row boolean array swapped row by row. The recurrence is identical to the 2D version but memory drops from quadratic to linear.

animation.hint: dp[i][j] tells whether s[:i] matches p[:j]; handle '*' as zero or repeat of the preceding char.

approaches.name: Backtracking with Used Set
approaches.idea: Build one permutation at a time by always picking the next unused number. A boolean used array tracks which indices are already placed; when the path is full the current permutation is saved, and the last choice is undone before trying the next candidate. This explores all orderings without repetition.
approaches.python:
def permutations_backtrack(nums):
    res = []

    def backtrack(path, used):
        if len(path) == len(nums):
            res.append(list(path))
            return
        for i, num in enumerate(nums):
            if used[i]:
                continue
            used[i] = True
            path.append(num)
            backtrack(path, used)
            path.pop()
            used[i] = False

    backtrack([], [False] * len(nums))
    return res


print(permutations_backtrack([1, 2, 3]))

approaches.name: Swap-Based Backtracking
approaches.idea: Fix a position start and, for every index i from start onward, swap nums[start] with nums[i], recurse on the next position, then swap back. When start reaches the end the array itself holds one complete permutation. No extra visited array is required because swapping explores each unused element exactly once.

approaches.name: Iterative Insertion
approaches.idea: Start with a single empty permutation and, for each incoming number, insert it at every possible position of every existing permutation to produce the next generation of permutations. After the last number is inserted all n! permutations have been materialized. This is a breadth-first build-up instead of depth-first search.

animation.hint: Place each unused number into the next slot, then recurse and undo the placement.

approaches.name: Sorted Keys with Floor Lookup
approaches.idea: Store each key's history with timestamps kept in sorted order. set() appends at the end because timestamps arrive strictly increasing, and get() performs a floor lookup that returns the newest value whose timestamp does not exceed the query. Python uses bisect over parallel lists while Java uses a TreeMap with floorEntry.
approaches.time: set O(log t), get O(log t)
approaches.python:
import bisect


class TimeMap:
    def __init__(self):
        self.data = {}

    def set(self, key, value, timestamp):
        entry = self.data.setdefault(key, [[], []])
        entry[0].append(timestamp)
        entry[1].append(value)

    def get(self, key, timestamp):
        entry = self.data.get(key)
        if entry is None:
            return ""
        timestamps, values = entry
        idx = bisect.bisect_right(timestamps, timestamp) - 1
        return values[idx] if idx >= 0 else ""


tm = TimeMap()
tm.set("foo", "bar", 1)
print(tm.get("foo", 1))
print(tm.get("foo", 3))
tm.set("foo", "bar2", 4)
print(tm.get("foo", 4))
print(tm.get("foo", 5))
print(tm.get("foo", 0))

approaches.name: Manual Binary Search
approaches.idea: Keep an ordered list of (timestamp, value) entries per key and hand-roll a binary search for the rightmost entry whose timestamp is at most the query. This makes the floor logic fully explicit: it converges on the answer by repeatedly halving the search interval and remembers the last valid value seen.

approaches.name: Linear Scan from Newest
approaches.idea: Store each key's entries as a plain list and, on get(), walk backwards from the most recent entry until a timestamp at most the query is found. It is the simplest implementation with an O(t) lookup per query, illustrating the correctness trade-off versus binary search.

animation.hint: For each key keep timestamps sorted and binary search the largest timestamp <= query.

approaches.name: Triple Reversal
approaches.idea: Reverse the whole array once, then reverse the first k elements and finally the last n-k elements. Composing these three segment reversals shifts every element to the right by k positions in constant extra space. The trick works because reversing twice restores in-place order inside each segment while globally swapping the two halves.
approaches.python:
def rotate_reverse(nums, k):
    n = len(nums)
    k %= n
    if k == 0:
        return nums

    def reverse(lo, hi):
        while lo < hi:
            nums[lo], nums[hi] = nums[hi], nums[lo]
            lo += 1
            hi -= 1

    reverse(0, n - 1)
    reverse(0, k - 1)
    reverse(k, n - 1)
    return nums


print(rotate_reverse([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7], 3))

approaches.name: Cyclic Replacement (Juggling)
approaches.idea: Walk the array in cycles: each element moves to (current + k) mod n, displacing the element already there, which is then moved to its own destination, and so on. Because the number of independent cycles equals gcd(n, k), repeating this from each cycle start covers every element exactly once with O(1) extra memory.
approaches.python:
from math import gcd


def rotate_cycles(nums, k):
    n = len(nums)
    k %= n
    if k == 0:
        return nums
    moved = 0
    start = 0
    while moved < n:
        current = start
        prev = nums[start]
        while True:
            next_idx = (current + k) % n
            nums[next_idx], prev = prev, nums[next_idx]
            current = next_idx
            moved += 1
            if current == start:
                break
        start += 1
    return nums


print(rotate_cycles([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7], 3))

approaches.name: Extra Array Copy
approaches.idea: Allocate a second array and place every element at its rotated index rotated[(i + k) mod n] = nums[i], then copy the result back. This is the most direct formulation of the problem and is easy to verify, at the cost of linear auxiliary memory.
approaches.python:
def rotate_extra(nums, k):
    n = len(nums)
    k %= n
    if k == 0:
        return nums
    rotated = [0] * n
    for i in range(n):
        rotated[(i + k) % n] = nums[i]
    nums[:] = rotated
    return nums


print(rotate_extra([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7], 3))

animation.hint: Reverse the whole array, then reverse the first k and the last n-k segments.

approaches.name: Split, Reverse, Join
approaches.idea: Split the input into words using whitespace as the delimiter, reverse the order of the resulting list, and join the words back with single spaces. This is the shortest, most declarative solution and leans on the standard library for tokenizing and joining.

approaches.name: In-Place Character Reversal
approaches.idea: Convert the string to a character array and reverse the entire array, then reverse the characters within each individual word. The first pass flips the word order and the second pass un-flips each word's letters, restoring normal spelling while keeping the new order. No split or extra token storage is needed.

approaches.name: Word Stack
approaches.idea: Scan the string one character at a time, accumulating characters into a word buffer and pushing each finished word onto a stack when a space is hit. Popping the stack yields the words in reversed order, and they are joined with single spaces. This handles arbitrary spacing robustly.

animation.hint: Reverse the whole string, then reverse each individual word to fix the letters.

approaches.name: Recursive Post-order DFS
approaches.idea: Each node reports the maximum 'gain' a single downward branch through it can contribute (clamped at zero so paths can start anywhere). A shared best-so-far combines the left branch, the node itself, and the right branch, so the optimal path through every node is evaluated exactly once.

approaches.name: Iterative Post-order with Stack
approaches.idea: Simulates the recursion using an explicit stack of (node, visited) pairs. On the second visit both children have already been resolved, so the max gain per node and the best path through it can be formed in true post-order without any recursion.

approaches.name: Reversed Pre-order Accumulation
approaches.idea: A pre-order walk collects nodes parent-before-child; children therefore appear after their parent in the list. Processing the reversed list guarantees every child is resolved before its parent, so gains and the best path can be accumulated bottom-up using only a single stack plus the collected order.
approaches.python:
class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right


def max_path_sum(root):
    best = float("-inf")
    order = []
    stack = [root]
    while stack:
        node = stack.pop()
        if node is None:
            continue
        order.append(node)
        stack.append(node.left)
        stack.append(node.right)
    gain = {}
    for node in reversed(order):
        left = max(gain.get(node.left, 0), 0)
        right = max(gain.get(node.right, 0), 0)
        best = max(best, left + node.val + right)
        gain[node] = node.val + max(left, right)
    return best


root = TreeNode(-10, TreeNode(9), TreeNode(20, TreeNode(15), TreeNode(7)))
print(max_path_sum(root))

animation.hint: Watch the gain value each node reports climb up the tree while best tracks the largest left+node+right sum seen.

approaches.name: Reverse the Whole Number
approaches.idea: Rebuild the integer digit by digit in reverse order using repeated modulo and division by 10, then compare the rebuilt number with the original. Negatives are rejected immediately because a minus sign can never be mirrored by digits alone.

approaches.name: Reverse Only Half the Number
approaches.idea: Reverse only the second half of the digits while the first half is being divided away. The number is a palindrome when the remaining first half equals the reversed second half (for even length) or equals it after dropping the middle digit (for odd length).

approaches.name: String Two Pointer
approaches.idea: Convert the integer to its decimal string and place one pointer at each end. Compare the characters while moving the pointers inward; any mismatch means the number is not a palindrome.
approaches.time: O(d) where d = number of digits

animation.hint: Watch reversed_num grow from the trailing digits while the two pointers squeeze in from both ends of the string.

approaches.name: Multi-source BFS with Timestamps
approaches.idea: Seed a queue with every rotten orange at time 0, then spread to fresh neighbors while storing the current minute on each cell. The answer is the largest timestamp ever assigned, provided no fresh orange remains unreached.

approaches.name: Level-by-Level BFS
approaches.idea: Run a breadth-first flood where each full layer of the queue corresponds to exactly one minute. The minute counter is incremented once per layer, so the total time is the number of levels needed to rot all reachable fresh oranges.

approaches.name: DFS Time Flooding
approaches.idea: Flood the grid from every rotten orange with a recursive 'time' function that records the earliest minute each cell is reached. A cell keeps the minimum of all arriving times, and the final answer is the largest recorded finite time; any fresh cell left at infinity means the answer is -1.

animation.hint: Watch the orange cells flip from 1 to 2 outward in rings, one ring per minute, as the frontier grows.

approaches.name: Top-down Memoized Recursion
approaches.idea: At each position the number of ways to finish is the sum of ways(i+1) for a single digit 1-9 plus ways(i+2) when the two-digit number is between 10 and 26. A memo dict stores already computed positions so overlapping subproblems are solved once.

approaches.name: Bottom-up Tabulation
approaches.idea: Fill a dp array left to right where dp[i] is the number of ways to decode the first i characters. Each cell is built from dp[i-1] when the new single digit is valid and from dp[i-2] when the previous pair forms a valid letter.

approaches.name: Space-optimized Rolling DP
approaches.idea: The recurrence only needs the two most recent dp values, so instead of an array only prev2 and prev1 are carried forward. This keeps the same Fibonacci-like logic while dropping the working memory to constant space.

animation.hint: Watch each dp[i] accumulate contributions from taking one digit and from taking a valid two-digit pair.

approaches.name: Linear Scan
approaches.idea: Try every possible eating speed from 1 up to the largest pile and compute the total hours needed as the sum of ceiling(pile / speed). Return the first speed that finishes within the allowed hours.

approaches.name: Binary Search
approaches.idea: The feasibility predicate 'hours(speed) <= h' is monotone, so the minimum speed is found by binary searching the range 1..max(piles), shrinking the upper bound when a speed works and raising the lower bound otherwise.

approaches.name: Exponential Search
approaches.idea: First double the candidate speed (1, 2, 4, ...) until it becomes feasible, which finds a tight range around the answer quickly. Then run the same binary search inside that narrow bracket, saving work when the answer is small.

animation.hint: Watch low and high close in on the smallest speed whose summed hours still fit inside the deadline.

approaches.name: Expand Around Center
approaches.idea: Every palindrome has a center, either a single character (odd length) or the gap between two characters (even length). From each of the 2n-1 centers, expand outward while the characters match and count every palindrome produced.
approaches.python:
def count_palindromic_substrings(s):
    n = len(s)
    total = 0
    for center in range(2 * n - 1):
        left = center // 2
        right = left + center % 2
        while left >= 0 and right < n and s[left] == s[right]:
            total += 1
            left -= 1
            right += 1
    return total


print(count_palindromic_substrings("aaa"))

approaches.name: Dynamic Programming Table
approaches.idea: A boolean table marks substrings that are palindromes; a substring is a palindrome when its endpoints match and its interior is a palindrome. Iterate by increasing length and count every true cell.

approaches.name: Manacher's Algorithm
approaches.idea: Transform the string by inserting sentinels so every palindrome becomes odd-length, then compute the longest palindrome radius centered at each position in linear time by mirroring against the current rightmost boundary. The number of palindromes centered at a position equals (radius + 1) // 2.

animation.hint: Watch the total counter tick up once per successful expansion while each center scans outward symmetrically.

approaches.name: 2D Dynamic Programming
approaches.idea: Let dp[r][c] hold the side length of the largest all-ones square whose bottom-right corner is (r, c). A 1 cell takes 1 plus the minimum of its top, left, and diagonal neighbors, and the largest dp value squared is the answer.

approaches.name: Space-optimized 1D DP
approaches.idea: The recurrence for row r only needs the previous row, so a single dp array is reused while a prev variable remembers the diagonal value from the row above. This is the same transition logic with constant working memory.
approaches.python:
def maximal_square(matrix):
    rows, cols = len(matrix), len(matrix[0])
    dp = [0] * (cols + 1)
    best = 0
    for r in range(rows):
        prev = 0
        for c in range(1, cols + 1):
            temp = dp[c]
            if matrix[r][c - 1] == "1":
                dp[c] = min(dp[c], dp[c - 1], prev) + 1
                best = max(best, dp[c])
            else:
                dp[c] = 0
            prev = temp
    return best * best


matrix = ["10100", "10111", "11111", "10010"]
print(maximal_square(matrix))

approaches.name: Binary Search with Prefix Sums
approaches.idea: Build a prefix-sum grid that answers 'how many ones are in any rectangle' in O(1). Then binary search the largest feasible side length k, checking whether any k-by-k rectangle is full of ones.

animation.hint: Watch the dp cells grow as each 1 takes the minimum of its up, left, and diagonal neighbors plus one.

approaches.name: Trie + Backtracking DFS
approaches.idea: Insert every word into a trie, then run a depth-first search from each board cell that only follows children present in the trie. A word is collected when a trie node marked as a word is reached, and cells are temporarily marked visited during recursion.

approaches.name: Per-word Backtracking
approaches.idea: Skip the trie entirely: for each word independently run the classic Word Search backtracking that tries every starting cell and walks the four directions while characters match. Words that complete are added to the result.

approaches.name: Trie DFS with Branch Pruning
approaches.idea: Same trie-guided search, but every matched word is also deleted from the trie by recursively pruning child nodes that no longer carry any words. Consumed prefixes disappear from the structure so later searches skip already-found words automatically.

animation.hint: Follow the highlighted path across the grid as it descends the trie, and watch matched words vanish from the structure.

approaches.name: HashSet Cycle Detection
approaches.idea: Repeatedly replace the number by the sum of the squares of its digits and record every value in a set. If we reach 1 the number is happy; if we see a value again, a cycle has closed and the number can never reach 1.
approaches.python:
def is_happy(n):
    seen = set()
    while n != 1 and n not in seen:
        seen.add(n)
        n = sum(int(d) ** 2 for d in str(n))
    return n == 1


print(is_happy(19))

approaches.name: Floyd's Tortoise and Hare
approaches.idea: Run two pointers, one advancing one step and the other two steps per iteration. Because the process either lands on 1 or enters a cycle, the fast pointer will either hit 1 or meet the slow pointer; meeting without hitting 1 means the number is unhappy.
approaches.python:
def is_happy(n):
    def next_val(x):
        total = 0
        while x > 0:
            digit = x % 10
            total += digit * digit
            x //= 10
        return total

    slow = n
    fast = next_val(n)
    while fast != 1 and slow != fast:
        slow = next_val(slow)
        fast = next_val(next_val(fast))
    return fast == 1


print(is_happy(19))

approaches.name: Known-Cycle Short-Circuit
approaches.idea: It is a proven fact that the only cycle in this process contains 4. Keep applying the digit-square sum and stop as soon as the value is 1 or 4; arriving at 4 proves the number will loop forever and is therefore unhappy.

animation.hint: Watch the set fill up with new sums until the chain either collapses to 1 or repeats a previously seen value.

approaches.name: Recursive In-order List
approaches.idea: An in-order traversal of a valid BST produces strictly increasing values. Collect the traversal into a list and verify that every adjacent pair is strictly ordered; any equal or descending step invalidates the tree.

approaches.name: Recursive Bounds Check
approaches.idea: Pass each node a (low, high) interval it must lie inside, shrinking the interval to (low, node.val) for the left child and (node.val, high) for the right. The tree is valid exactly when every node satisfies its interval.

approaches.name: Iterative In-order with Stack
approaches.idea: Emulate the in-order walk with an explicit stack, comparing each popped node against the previously visited node. The traversal is strictly increasing if and only if the tree is a valid BST, and no recursion is used.
approaches.python:
class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right


def is_valid_bst(root):
    stack = []
    node = root
    prev = None
    while stack or node is not None:
        while node is not None:
            stack.append(node)
            node = node.left
        node = stack.pop()
        if prev is not None and prev.val >= node.val:
            return False
        prev = node
        node = node.right
    return True


root = TreeNode(5, TreeNode(3, TreeNode(1), TreeNode(4)), TreeNode(7, TreeNode(6), TreeNode(8)))
print(is_valid_bst(root))

animation.hint: Watch the highlighted node move in in-order sequence and confirm each value is larger than prev.

approaches.name: Greedy (Farthest Reachable)
approaches.idea: Scan left to right tracking the farthest index reachable from the current window. Each time the scan reaches the end of the current jump, increment the jump count and expand the window to the farthest point seen so far. This produces the minimum number of jumps in a single linear pass.
approaches.python:
def jump(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    jumps = 0
    current_end = 0
    farthest = 0
    for i in range(n - 1):
        farthest = max(farthest, i + nums[i])
        if i == current_end:
            jumps += 1
            current_end = farthest
    return jumps


nums = [2, 3, 1, 1, 4]
print(jump(nums))

approaches.name: Dynamic Programming
approaches.idea: Let dp[i] be the fewest jumps needed to reach index i. Seed dp[0] = 0 and for every reachable index i update each landing spot i+1..i+nums[i] with dp[i]+1. It is slower but works for any reachability problem and is straightforward to reason about.

approaches.name: Backward Greedy
approaches.idea: Start at the last index and repeatedly jump to the leftmost index that can still reach the current position, counting one jump each time. Since each such jump is the furthest we can retreat for that cost, the total jump count is minimized.

animation.hint: Watch how the farthest reachable index advances each time the current jump window ends.

approaches.name: Binary Search
approaches.idea: A peak always exists because the array is bounded by negative infinity. Compare the middle element with its right neighbor: if the middle is larger, a peak lies in the left half, otherwise in the right half. This halves the search range every step.

approaches.name: Linear Scan
approaches.idea: Simply walk through the array and return the first index whose element is greater than its right neighbor. If no such index exists the last element must be a peak. Simple and correct for small inputs.

approaches.name: Divide and Conquer
approaches.idea: Recursively solve the same peak-finding problem on the chosen half of the array. The recursion mirrors the binary search decision but expresses it as two independent subproblems merged at the midpoint.

animation.hint: See the search window shrink while comparing the middle element with its right neighbor.

approaches.name: Dynamic Programming
approaches.idea: dp[i] stores the length of the longest increasing subsequence ending at i. Recompute dp[i] by scanning all previous indices and taking the best dp[j]+1 where nums[j] < nums[i]. The answer is the maximum over all dp values.

approaches.name: Patience Sorting
approaches.idea: Keep a tails array where tails[k] is the smallest possible tail of an increasing subsequence of length k+1. For each number, binary search the first tails entry >= it and replace it; if none, append. The final length of tails is the answer.

approaches.name: Memoized Recursion
approaches.idea: Define dfs(i) as the longest increasing subsequence starting at i, choosing any later index j with nums[i] < nums[j]. A memo table caches results so each index is computed only once, trading recursion depth for speed.

title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree

approaches.name: Recursive DFS
approaches.idea: Recursively search both subtrees for p and q. A node whose left and right subtrees each contain one of the targets is the lowest common ancestor; if only one side finds anything, that result propagates upward. Clean and canonical.

class TreeNode:

        self.left = None
        self.right = None


def lowest_common_ancestor(root, p, q):
    if root is None or root is p or root is q:
        return root
    left = lowest_common_ancestor(root.left, p, q)
    right = lowest_common_ancestor(root.right, p, q)
    if left is not None and right is not None:
        return root
    return left if left is not None else right

approaches.idea: Traverse the tree once recording each node's parent in a map until both p and q are discovered. Then climb from p up to the root, marking every ancestor, and climb from q until hitting a marked node. That node is the LCA.

approaches.name: Root-to-Node Paths

approaches.name: Fixed Array Children
approaches.idea: Each trie node keeps an array of 26 child pointers plus an isEnd flag. Descend one level per character by indexing children[ord(c)-ord('a')]. Fastest lookups since child access is a direct array index.

approaches.name: HashMap Children
approaches.idea: Each node keeps a dictionary mapping a character to its child node. Child lookup is O(1) on average but memory only grows for characters actually used, which helps when the alphabet is large or sparse.

approaches.name: Prefix Set Store

approaches.name: Iterative Exponentiation by Squaring
approaches.idea: Rewrite x^n using the binary representation of n. Square x each step and multiply it into the result only when the current bit of n is 1. Handles negative n by inverting x first.

approaches.name: Recursive Exponentiation by Squaring
approaches.idea: Split the problem into halves with the recurrence x^n = (x^(n/2))^2, and multiply once more when n is odd. Negative exponents are flipped into a reciprocal of a positive-power call.

approaches.name: Naive Repeated Multiplication
approaches.idea: Multiply x by itself |n| times accumulating into a running product, then take the reciprocal if n is negative. Not scalable for large exponents but is the baseline definition of the operation.

approaches.name: Two Pointers
approaches.idea: Use a read pointer that scans every element and a write pointer that marks where the next unique value belongs. Because the input is sorted, uniqueness is detected by comparing with the last written value. Works fully in place.

approaches.idea: For every unvisited land cell, flood-fill its whole island with recursion, summing 1 for each cell and sinking it to water so it is never counted twice. Keep the running maximum island size.

def max_area_of_island(grid):

    cols = len(grid[0])

        if r < 0 or r >= rows or c < 0 or c >= cols or grid[r][c] == 0:

        grid[r][c] = 0
        area = 1
        area += dfs(r + 1, c)
        area += dfs(r - 1, c)
        area += dfs(r, c + 1)
        area += dfs(r, c - 1)
        return area

    best = 0
    for r in range(rows):
        for c in range(cols):
            if grid[r][c] == 1:
                best = max(best, dfs(r, c))
    return best

approaches.name: Deque of Timestamps
approaches.idea: Append each hit's timestamp to the back of a deque. On getHits, drop every timestamp at the front that is more than 300 seconds old and return the remaining length. Clean, exact, and amortized O(1) per hit.

approaches.name: Circular Bucket Array
approaches.idea: Use 300 slots indexed by timestamp % 300. Each slot records the last timestamp it was used for and a count; a slot is reused when a hit arrives at the same timestamp. getHits sums the counts of all slots still inside the window.
approaches.time: O(1) per hit, O(300) per query

approaches.name: Sorted List with Binary Search
approaches.idea: Keep timestamps in a grow-only sorted list and answer getHits by binary searching for the first timestamp >= now-299. The number of hits in range is simply the list length minus that index.
approaches.time: O(1) per hit, O(log n) per query

import bisect


class HitCounter:
    def __init__(self):
        self.timestamps = []

    def hit(self, timestamp):
        self.timestamps.append(timestamp)

    def get_hits(self, timestamp):
        start = bisect.bisect_left(self.timestamps, timestamp - 299)
        return len(self.timestamps) - start

approaches.name: Boyer-Moore Voting
approaches.idea: Maintain a candidate and a counter. When the counter is zero adopt the current element as candidate; then increment for a match or decrement otherwise. Since the majority element appears more than n/2 times it survives as the final candidate.

approaches.name: Hash Map Counting
approaches.idea: Count the frequency of every element in a dictionary. Stop as soon as some count exceeds n/2 and return that element. Simple and general even when no majority is guaranteed.

approaches.name: Sorting
approaches.idea: Sort the array in place and return the element at index n/2. Any majority element must occupy the middle position of the sorted array because it spans more than half of the positions.

def majority_element(nums):

    return nums[len(nums) // 2]

approaches.name: String reversal with sign handling
approaches.idea: Take the absolute value, reverse its decimal digits as a string, strip leading zeros and reattach the sign. An overflow check against the 32-bit signed bounds decides whether to return 0. This relies on the runtime's string utilities to do the digit work.
approaches.python:
INT_MAX = 2**31 - 1
INT_MIN = -2**31


def reverse_string(x):
    sign = -1 if x < 0 else 1
    digits = str(abs(x))[::-1].lstrip('0') or '0'
    result = sign * int(digits)
    return 0 if result > INT_MAX or result < INT_MIN else result


print(reverse_string(123))

approaches.name: Digit pop-and-push loop
approaches.idea: Repeatedly pop the last decimal digit of the absolute value and push it onto a running result (result = result * 10 + digit). Before pushing, check that result * 10 + digit cannot exceed the 32-bit bound, which catches overflow without needing big integers.
approaches.python:
INT_MAX = 2**31 - 1
INT_MIN = -2**31


def reverse_pop_push(x):
    sign = -1 if x < 0 else 1
    n = abs(x)
    result = 0
    while n > 0:
        digit = n % 10
        if result > (INT_MAX - digit) // 10:
            return 0
        result = result * 10 + digit
        n //= 10
    return sign * result


print(reverse_pop_push(123))

approaches.name: Recursive digit building
approaches.idea: A recursive helper consumes one digit at a time from the remaining number and accumulates the reversed value, building it from the least-significant digit upwards. The base case returns the accumulated value once all digits are consumed; overflow is checked only at the end.

animation.hint: Watch the digit that gets moved to the front of the result on each step.

approaches.name: Prefix sums with linear scan
approaches.idea: Build a prefix-sum array over the weights and draw one uniform random integer in [1, total]. Walk the prefix array from left to right and return the first index whose prefix is at least the random value. Straightforward but scans in O(n) per query.

import random


def pick_linear(weights):
    prefix = []
    acc = 0
    for w in weights:
        acc += w
        prefix.append(acc)
    r = random.randint(1, acc)
    for i, p in enumerate(prefix):
        if r <= p:
            return i
    return len(weights) - 1

approaches.name: Rejection sampling
approaches.idea: Propose a uniformly random index and independently a random threshold below the maximum weight; accept the index if its weight beats the threshold. Every index is chosen in proportion to its weight, and the loop simply retries rejected proposals.

animation.hint: Watch the random point land inside the cumulative weight range that maps to a specific index.

approaches.name: Stack simulation
approaches.idea: Iterate over the asteroids and push each one onto a stack. Whenever the top of the stack is moving right and the new asteroid moves left, they collide: the smaller one explodes, equal sizes both explode, and the survivor keeps checking against the new top. The stack holds the final survivors in order.

approaches.name: In-place array as stack
approaches.idea: Reuse the input array itself as the stack by keeping a write pointer. New asteroids are written at the write position and collisions shrink the pointer back, so survivors overwrite earlier entries. No extra memory beyond the input, and the valid prefix is sliced off at the end.

approaches.name: Recursive elimination
approaches.idea: Scan the list for the first adjacent collision (a positive asteroid directly followed by a negative one), remove both when equal or the smaller survivor otherwise, and recursively resolve the shortened list. The recursion restarts after every removal so chains of explosions are handled naturally.

animation.hint: Follow the top of the stack as the new asteroid either destroys it, survives, or both vanish.

approaches.name: Full copy brute force
approaches.idea: Take a snapshot of the matrix, then scan the snapshot for zeros. Whenever the copy holds a zero, zero out that entire row and column in the original matrix. Simple and obviously correct because decisions are made from the untouched copy, at the cost of O(mn) memory.

approaches.name: Row and column mark sets
approaches.idea: Collect the indices of every row and column that contain a zero into two sets during one scan. A second pass blanks whole rows and columns purely from those sets, so each cell is only written once. Uses O(m+n) memory instead of a full copy.

approaches.name: First row/column in-place markers
approaches.idea: Use the first row and first column as marker storage: record which rows and columns contain zeros there, remembering whether the first row/column themselves held a zero. Then zero the interior cells from the markers and finally handle the first row/column. No extra memory beyond a couple of booleans.

animation.hint: Watch the zeros cascade through their entire row and column.

approaches.name: Recursive parenthesized evaluation
approaches.idea: Parse the string with a recursive descent over a shared position index. A helper evaluates one term until a closing parenthesis or the end, recursing whenever it hits an open parenthesis. The recursion naturally captures the nesting depth of the expression.

approaches.name: Single stack with sign accumulation
approaches.idea: Keep a running result and a running sign. Digits are folded into a number, '+'/'-' flush the current number into the result and update the sign, and '(' pushes the current result and sign so the inner expression starts fresh; on ')' the saved sign and result are restored. Each parenthesis adds constant stack work.
approaches.python:
def calculate_stack(s):
    stack = []
    result = 0
    sign = 1
    num = 0
    for ch in s:
        if ch.isdigit():
            num = num * 10 + int(ch)
        elif ch in '+-':
            result += sign * num
            num = 0
            sign = 1 if ch == '+' else -1
        elif ch == '(':
            stack.append(result)
            stack.append(sign)
            result = 0
            sign = 1
        elif ch == ')':
            result += sign * num
            num = 0
            result *= stack.pop()
            result += stack.pop()
            sign = 1
    return result + sign * num


print(calculate_stack("(1+(4+5+2)-3)+(6+8)"))

approaches.name: Two stacks (operators and operands)
approaches.idea: A classic operator-precedence evaluator: numbers go on an operand stack, '+'/'-' and parentheses go on an operator stack. When a closing parenthesis or a new operator arrives, pending operators are applied to the top two operands first. This generalizes cleanly to expressions with multiple precedence levels.

animation.hint: Each open parenthesis pushes the accumulated total and sign so the inner expression can start over.

approaches.name: HashMap node-to-clone
approaches.idea: First pass creates a clone node for every original node and maps original to clone in a hash map. Second pass wires up each clone's next and random by looking up the corresponding clone of the original pointers. Clear and simple, but uses O(n) extra space for the map.
approaches.python:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None, random=None):

        self.next = next
        self.random = random


def build_sample():

    n3 = Node(10)
    n4 = Node(1)
    n0.next = n1
    n1.next = n2
    n2.next = n3
    n3.next = n4
    n1.random = n0
    n2.random = n4
    n3.random = n2
    n4.random = n0
    return n0


def list_repr(head):
    out = []
    cur = head
    while cur:
        out.append([cur.val, cur.random.val if cur.random else None])
        cur = cur.next
    return out


def copy_with_map(head):
    if head is None:
        return None
    lookup = {}
    cur = head
    while cur:
        lookup[cur] = Node(cur.val)
        cur = cur.next
    cur = head
    while cur:
        lookup[cur].next = lookup.get(cur.next)
        lookup[cur].random = lookup.get(cur.random)
        cur = cur.next
    return lookup[head]


print(list_repr(copy_with_map(build_sample())))

approaches.name: Interleaved clones (O(1) space)
approaches.idea: Insert each clone immediately after its original (A-A'-B-B'-...), then set every clone's random to the clone of the original's random, and finally unweave the doubled list back into the original and the copy. Achieves a deep copy with only constant extra memory.

    cur = head

approaches.name: Preorder DFS with null markers
approaches.idea: Serialize with a preorder traversal that writes 'null' for empty children, producing a string like '1,2,null,null,3,4,null,null,5,null,null'. Deserialization replays that preorder with a shared index, building nodes recursively and consuming one token per null or value.

class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right


def build_sample():

    root.left = TreeNode(2)
    root.right = TreeNode(3)
    root.right.left = TreeNode(4)
    root.right.right = TreeNode(5)
    return root


def serialize_preorder(root):
    parts = []

    def dfs(node):
        if node is None:
            parts.append('null')
            return
        parts.append(str(node.val))
        dfs(node.left)
        dfs(node.right)

    dfs(root)
    return ','.join(parts)


def deserialize_preorder(data):
    tokens = data.split(',')
    index = [0]

    def build():
        token = tokens[index[0]]
        index[0] += 1
        if token == 'null':
            return None
        node = TreeNode(int(token))
        node.left = build()
        node.right = build()
        return node

    return build()


def collect_preorder(root):
    out = []

    def dfs(node):
        if node is None:
            out.append('null')
            return
        out.append(str(node.val))
        dfs(node.left)
        dfs(node.right)

    dfs(root)
    return out


data = serialize_preorder(build_sample())
print(data)
print(collect_preorder(deserialize_preorder(data)))

approaches.name: BFS level-order with queue
approaches.idea: Serialize breadth-first, writing each node's value (or 'null') as it is dequeued and enqueueing its children. Deserialization walks the token stream with a queue, attaching left and right children to each node as they appear. Naturally self-terminating since every node consumes exactly two tokens.
approaches.python:
from collections import deque


class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right


def build_sample():
    root = TreeNode(1)
    root.left = TreeNode(2)
    root.right = TreeNode(3)
    root.right.left = TreeNode(4)
    root.right.right = TreeNode(5)
    return root


def serialize_bfs(root):
    if root is None:
        return ''
    parts = []
    queue = deque([root])
    while queue:
        node = queue.popleft()
        if node is None:
            parts.append('null')
            continue
        parts.append(str(node.val))
        queue.append(node.left)
        queue.append(node.right)
    return ','.join(parts)


def deserialize_bfs(data):
    if data == '':
        return None
    tokens = data.split(',')
    root = TreeNode(int(tokens[0]))
    queue = deque([root])
    index = 1
    while queue and index < len(tokens):
        node = queue.popleft()
        if tokens[index] != 'null':
            node.left = TreeNode(int(tokens[index]))
            queue.append(node.left)
        index += 1
        if index < len(tokens) and tokens[index] != 'null':
            node.right = TreeNode(int(tokens[index]))
            queue.append(node.right)
        index += 1
    return root


def collect_preorder(root):
    out = []

    def dfs(node):
        if node is None:
            out.append('null')
            return
        out.append(str(node.val))
        dfs(node.left)
        dfs(node.right)

    dfs(root)
    return out


data = serialize_bfs(build_sample())
print(data)
print(collect_preorder(deserialize_bfs(data)))

approaches.name: Bracket-grouped notation
approaches.idea: Encode each node as its value followed by optional parenthesized subtrees, e.g. '1(2)(3(4)(5))', omitting groups entirely for missing children. Deserialization is a tiny recursive parser with a shared index that builds children whenever it sees an open parenthesis. Compact output with no 'null' markers.

animation.hint: Watch the traversal that turns the tree into a token stream, and back again.

approaches.name: DFS with cycle detection
approaches.idea: Compare consecutive words to harvest ordering constraints into an adjacency map, then topologically sort with a recursive DFS using three states (unvisited, in-progress, done). An in-progress edge signals a cycle and returns an empty string; the valid order is the reverse of the finishing order.

approaches.name: Kahn's BFS with indegrees
approaches.idea: Build the same constraint graph, then count indegrees and seed a queue with all zero-indegree characters. Repeatedly pop a character, append it to the order, and decrement its neighbors' indegrees, enqueueing any that hit zero. If fewer characters are output than exist, a cycle prevents a total order.

approaches.name: Transitive-closure matrix sort
approaches.idea: Put every distinct character into a matrix and record pairwise less-than relations found between consecutive words. Compute the transitive closure with Floyd-Warshall, then read the order by repeatedly picking the character with the smallest number of predecessors. A symmetric closure entry signals a cycle.

animation.hint: Watch constraints turn into directed edges that order the alien alphabet.

title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array

approaches.name: Binary search on the rotation point
approaches.idea: The array is two increasing runs stitched at the rotation. Compare the middle element against the right endpoint: if the middle is larger, the drop (and hence the minimum) lies to the right; otherwise the minimum is at or to the left. Shrink the search window until it is a single element.

approaches.name: Linear scan
approaches.idea: Walk the array once and remember the smallest value seen so far. Because the rotated array has exactly one descent, the first element is only ever beaten by the true minimum right after the rotation. Straightforward and O(n), but it inspects every element.

approaches.name: Divide-and-conquer recursion
approaches.idea: Recursively split the range in half and return the smaller of the two halves' minima. A fast-path returns the left element immediately whenever the subrange is already strictly increasing (nums[lo] < nums[hi]), which prunes the unrotated side. The base case is a single element.

animation.hint: Watch the search window tighten around the single element where the array drops.

approaches.name: Monotonic increasing stack
approaches.idea: Keep a stack of bar indices with strictly increasing heights. When a bar is shorter than the stack top, pop the top and treat it as the rectangle height, with its width bounded by the new top and the current index. A sentinel 0 at the end forces the stack to flush completely.
approaches.python:
def largest_rectangle_stack(heights):
    heights = heights + [0]
    stack = []
    max_area = 0
    for i, h in enumerate(heights):
        while stack and heights[stack[-1]] >= h:
            height = heights[stack.pop()]
            width = i if not stack else i - stack[-1] - 1
            max_area = max(max_area, height * width)
        stack.append(i)
    return max_area


print(largest_rectangle_stack([2, 1, 5, 6, 2, 3]))

approaches.name: Expand-around-each-bar brute force
approaches.idea: For every bar, treat its height as the rectangle height and walk left and right while neighboring bars are at least that tall to find the widest possible span. The area height * span is compared against the running maximum. Intuitive but quadratic because each bar does a full scan in the worst case.

approaches.name: Divide and conquer at the minimum
approaches.idea: The best rectangle either spans the whole range, using the minimum bar as its height, or lies entirely to the left or right of that minimum. Find the minimum index in the current range, combine the three candidates recursively, and return the largest. Each level is a linear minimum search, giving O(n log n) overall.

animation.hint: Watch the popped bar close off its widest valid rectangle as a shorter bar arrives.

approaches.name: 2D Dynamic Programming Table
approaches.idea: Build a dp table where dp[r][c] counts paths to cell (r, c). Since movement is only right and down, every non-obstacle cell inherits the sum of the cells above and to its left. Obstacles zero out their cell. The bottom-right corner holds the answer.

approaches.name: Rolling 1D DP
approaches.idea: Only the previous row is ever needed, so a single array dp reused across rows gives the same recurrence with O(n) space. dp[c] is overwritten in place as each row is scanned left to right, representing the current row while referencing the already-updated left neighbor.

approaches.name: Memoized DFS
approaches.idea: A recursive search moves right or down and returns 0 when it leaves the grid or hits an obstacle and 1 at the goal. Results of subproblems are cached in a memo table so each cell is computed once. This is a top-down view of the same recurrence.

animation.hint: Watch the dp table fill as each cell sums its top and left neighbors.

approaches.name: Char-by-Char State Machine
approaches.idea: Scan the string in one pass: skip leading whitespace, read one sign character, then accumulate digits while guarding against overflow after each multiplication. If the running value would overflow the 32-bit range, return the clamped limit immediately. Any non-digit ends the parse.

approaches.name: Regex Extraction
approaches.idea: Use a regular expression that matches optional leading whitespace, an optional sign, and a run of digits at the start of the string. Parse the captured token as an integer and clamp it into the 32-bit range. Regexes make the tokenization declarative and concise.

approaches.name: Strip and Digit Accumulation
approaches.idea: Trim leading whitespace and the sign, then extract the whole run of leading digits as a token before converting it. The full magnitude is computed first and clamped afterwards, so overflow is handled at the end instead of during the scan. A different data-flow order from the incremental scanner.

animation.hint: See whitespace, sign, and digits consumed before the integer is clamped to 32 bits.

approaches.name: Floyd's Tortoise and Hare
approaches.idea: Two pointers move at different speeds; slow advances one node and fast advances two per step. If a cycle exists the fast pointer eventually laps the slow pointer and they meet. If the fast pointer ever reaches the end of the list, there is no cycle.

approaches.name: Hash Set of Visited Nodes
approaches.idea: Walk the list and insert every node reference into a hash set. If a node is already in the set before being added, the traversal has re-entered a previous node, proving a cycle exists. A tail that reaches null means the list is acyclic.

approaches.name: Brent's Cycle Detection
approaches.idea: A tortoise pointer teleports at increasing powers of two while a hare moves one step at a time. Each time the tortoise jumps, the step counter doubles, so the hare never travels more than twice the cycle length before they meet. Constant extra space with a different stepping scheme than Floyd's algorithm.

animation.hint: Watch the slow and fast pointers — they only meet if a cycle exists.

approaches.name: Square and Sort
approaches.idea: The naive approach squares every element into a new list and then sorts it with the built-in sort. Since squaring destroys the original ordering, the result must be resorted. Simple and correct, but it pays an extra O(n log n) factor for the sort.

approaches.name: Two Pointers from Both Ends
approaches.idea: Because the input is sorted, the largest absolute value is at one of the two ends. A left and a right pointer compare absolute values, write the larger square into the back of the result array, and move inward. The result is built largest-first in a single linear pass.
approaches.python:
def sorted_squares_two_pointers(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    result = [0] * n
    left = 0
    right = n - 1
    for pos in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        if abs(nums[left]) > abs(nums[right]):
            result[pos] = nums[left] * nums[left]
            left += 1
        else:
            result[pos] = nums[right] * nums[right]
            right -= 1
    return result

nums = [-4, -1, 0, 3, 10]
print(sorted_squares_two_pointers(nums))

approaches.name: Split-Point Merge
approaches.idea: Find the boundary where the array switches from negative to non-negative. Walking left from the boundary yields squares in ascending order and walking right does the same, so the two sorted sequences are merged with two pointers. This linear merge is a fundamentally different strategy than filling from the outside in.
approaches.python:
def sorted_squares_merge(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    split = 0
    while split < n and nums[split] < 0:
        split += 1
    result = []
    negative = split - 1
    positive = split
    while negative >= 0 and positive < n:
        left_square = nums[negative] * nums[negative]
        right_square = nums[positive] * nums[positive]
        if left_square <= right_square:
            result.append(left_square)
            negative -= 1
        else:
            result.append(right_square)
            positive += 1
    while negative >= 0:
        result.append(nums[negative] * nums[negative])
        negative -= 1
    while positive < n:
        result.append(nums[positive] * nums[positive])
        positive += 1
    return result

nums = [-4, -1, 0, 3, 10]
print(sorted_squares_merge(nums))

animation.hint: Two pointers from both ends place the largest squares into the result first.

approaches.name: Frequency Sort
approaches.idea: Count each word with a hash map, then sort the distinct words by descending frequency with ascending lexicographic order as the tie-breaker. The first k entries of the sorted list are returned. Sorting all m distinct words is the simplest correct approach.
approaches.python:
from collections import Counter


def top_k_frequent_sort(words, k):
    counts = Counter(words)
    sorted_words = sorted(counts.items(), key=lambda item: (-item[1], item[0]))
    return [word for word, _ in sorted_words[:k]]

words = ["i", "love", "leetcode", "i", "love", "coding"]
print(top_k_frequent_sort(words, 2))

approaches.name: Max-Heap Selection
approaches.idea: After tallying frequencies, push every distinct word into a heap ordered by descending frequency and then ascending word. Popping k times pulls out the most frequent words in the required order without ever fully sorting the remaining ones. Heap selection is a different ranking mechanism than a comparison sort.
approaches.python:
import heapq
from collections import Counter


def top_k_frequent_heap(words, k):
    counts = Counter(words)
    heap = []
    for word, count in counts.items():
        heapq.heappush(heap, (-count, word))
    return [heapq.heappop(heap)[1] for _ in range(k)]

words = ["i", "love", "leetcode", "i", "love", "coding"]
print(top_k_frequent_heap(words, 2))

approaches.name: Bucket by Frequency
approaches.idea: Group distinct words into buckets indexed by their exact frequency using a hash map of lists. Then walk the buckets from the highest frequency downward, sorting each bucket lexicographically and collecting words until k have been taken. This exploits the bounded frequency range instead of doing a global sort.

animation.hint: Frequencies are tallied in a hash map and then ranked to pick the top k words.

approaches.name: Hash Set Lookup
approaches.idea: Load the first array into a hash set, then scan the second array and keep any element that is present in the set. A result set guarantees uniqueness. Simple hash-based membership testing with linear time.
approaches.python:
def intersection_hash(nums1, nums2):
    set1 = set(nums1)
    return [x for x in set(nums2) if x in set1]

nums1 = [1, 2, 2, 1]
nums2 = [2, 2]
print(intersection_hash(nums1, nums2))

approaches.name: Sort and Two Pointers
approaches.idea: Sort both arrays and walk them with two pointers, advancing the pointer of the smaller value each step. When the values are equal, record the element and skip all duplicates on both sides. No extra hash structure is needed beyond the result.
approaches.time: O(n log n + m log m)

approaches.name: Sort One Array and Binary Search
approaches.idea: Sort a single array and test each unique element of the other with binary search. Membership checks run in O(log n) each, trading the two-pointer merge for repeated half-interval probes. A fundamentally different lookup strategy on a sorted array.

animation.hint: Elements present in both arrays are collected into a result set.

approaches.name: Eager Recursive Flattening
approaches.idea: Flatten the entire nested structure into a plain list of integers once, in the constructor, using depth-first recursion. The iterator then simply serves values from the precomputed list with an index. Simple and fully eager, at the cost of O(n) upfront work and memory.

approaches.name: Lazy Stack of Frames
approaches.idea: Maintain a stack of (list, position) frames so only the currently visited list is expanded at any moment. When the active frame is exhausted it is popped and the next outer frame resumes. Work is deferred until next() is actually called, keeping the constructor O(1).
approaches.time: O(n) total, O(1) amortized per call

approaches.name: Generator Yielding / Reverse-Stack
approaches.idea: Treat flattening as a stream: Python uses a recursive generator that yields each integer and suspends, while Java pushes the nested elements in reverse onto a stack and expands top lists when hasNext() is polled. Integers are emitted lazily on demand with no precomputed list.
approaches.time: O(n) total, O(1) amortized per call

animation.hint: Nested lists are pushed and expanded on the stack so integers are yielded in order.

approaches.name: Custom Comparator Sort
approaches.idea: Convert every number to a string and sort them with a comparator that decides order by comparing concatenations a+b against b+a. After sorting, the strings are joined and any leading zero run is collapsed to a single zero. This is the classic one-pass comparison solution.
approaches.python:
from functools import cmp_to_key


def largest_number_sort(nums):
    def compare(a, b):
        if a + b > b + a:
            return -1
        if a + b < b + a:
            return 1
        return 0

    strings = [str(x) for x in nums]
    strings.sort(key=cmp_to_key(compare))
    result = "".join(strings)
    return "0" if result[0] == "0" else result

nums = [3, 30, 34, 5, 9]
print(largest_number_sort(nums))

approaches.name: Greedy Selection Sort
approaches.idea: Repeat the pairwise concatenation rule by scanning the remaining numbers and moving the winner of a+b vs b+a to the front each round. This is the same comparison relation applied by a manual O(n^2) selection sort instead of a library sort, so the ordering logic is spelled out step by step.
approaches.python:
def largest_number_selection(nums):
    remaining = [str(x) for x in nums]
    result = []
    while remaining:
        best_index = 0
        for i in range(1, len(remaining)):
            a = remaining[i]
            b = remaining[best_index]
            if a + b > b + a:
                best_index = i
        result.append(remaining.pop(best_index))
    answer = "".join(result)
    return "0" if answer[0] == "0" else answer

nums = [3, 30, 34, 5, 9]
print(largest_number_selection(nums))

approaches.name: Bubble Sort by Concatenation
approaches.idea: Apply the concatenation comparator as a bubble sort: repeatedly compare adjacent strings and swap when a+b is larger than b+a, until one pass makes no swaps. The rule is applied through local adjacent exchanges rather than a global ordering call. Same comparator, a third different sorting mechanism.
approaches.python:
def largest_number_bubble(nums):
    strings = [str(x) for x in nums]
    n = len(strings)
    for i in range(n):
        swapped = False
        for j in range(0, n - i - 1):
            a = strings[j]
            b = strings[j + 1]
            if b + a > a + b:
                strings[j], strings[j + 1] = strings[j + 1], strings[j]
                swapped = True
        if not swapped:
            break
    answer = "".join(strings)
    return "0" if answer[0] == "0" else answer

nums = [3, 30, 34, 5, 9]
print(largest_number_bubble(nums))

animation.hint: Numbers are reordered by their concatenation so the final joined string is largest.

approaches.name: Bitmask Enumeration
approaches.idea: Every subset corresponds to an n-bit mask where bit i selects element i. Iterate over all masks from 0 to 2^n-1 and collect the selected elements. This enumerates every combination through binary arithmetic rather than recursion.

approaches.name: Backtracking DFS
approaches.idea: A depth-first search builds subsets by deciding, for each starting index, whether to include the current element before recursing deeper. Every recursive entry records the current partial subset, and the stack unwinds after each choice. The recursion depth is bounded by the number of elements.
approaches.python:
def subsets_backtrack(nums):
    result = []
    current = []

    def dfs(start):
        result.append(current[:])
        for i in range(start, len(nums)):
            current.append(nums[i])
            dfs(i + 1)
            current.pop()

    dfs(0)
    return result

nums = [1, 2, 3]
print(subsets_backtrack(nums))

approaches.name: Iterative Expansion
approaches.idea: Start with the empty subset and grow it element by element. For each number, append a copy of every existing subset with the new number added, so the list of subsets doubles at every step. No recursion or bit manipulation is involved.
approaches.python:
def subsets_iterative(nums):
    result = [[]]
    for num in nums:
        result += [subset + [num] for subset in result]
    return result

nums = [1, 2, 3]
print(subsets_iterative(nums))

animation.hint: The DFS branches include or skip each element to build all subsets.

approaches.name: Split and Stack
approaches.idea: Split the path on slashes and push every non-empty, non-dot component onto a stack. A '..' pops the last component, while any other token is treated as a directory name and pushed. Finally join the stack contents with single slashes. This is the canonical token-and-stack approach.

approaches.name: Regex Tokenization and Stack
approaches.idea: Instead of splitting on slashes, use a regex that matches every run of characters between slashes to extract path tokens directly. The tokens then drive the same stack rules: ignore '.', pop on '..', push otherwise. The tokenizer itself differs — it never produces empty strings.

approaches.name: Char-by-Char State Machine
approaches.idea: Scan the path one character at a time, skipping slashes to read a token and then consuming until the next slash. Each completed token is processed against the stack, so no token array or regex is ever materialized. The components are parsed on the fly.

animation.hint: Components are pushed and popped by '..' to leave only the canonical path.

approaches.name: 2D Dynamic Programming
approaches.idea: Fill a table where dp[r][c] counts the distinct paths that reach cell (r, c). Because the robot can only move right or down, each cell's count is the sum of the count from above and the count from the left, with the first row and first column seeded with 1.

approaches.name: Combinatorics (Binomial Coefficient)
approaches.idea: Any valid route is a sequence of m-1 down moves and n-1 right moves. The number of distinct arrangements is therefore the binomial coefficient C(m+n-2, m-1), computed with exact integer arithmetic.

approaches.name: 1D Space-Optimized DP
approaches.idea: Roll the two-dimensional table into a single row array. Each iteration overwrites values in place so row[c] is the count from above (kept from the previous iteration) plus row[c-1] from the left, preserving the exact recurrence with a single array.

animation.hint: Watch dp fill from the top-left to the bottom-right as every cell sums its upper and left neighbors.

approaches.name: Backtracking with Hash-Set Constraints
approaches.idea: Backtrack over the empty cells in fixed order, trying digits 1-9. One set per row, column, and 3x3 box answers the 'already used' check in O(1), and failed digits are rolled back before trying the next one.
approaches.python:
def solve_sudoku(board):
    rows = [set() for _ in range(9)]
    cols = [set() for _ in range(9)]
    boxes = [set() for _ in range(9)]
    empty = []

    def box_index(r, c):
        return (r // 3) * 3 + c // 3

    for r in range(9):
        for c in range(9):
            val = board[r][c]
            if val == '.':
                empty.append((r, c))
            else:
                rows[r].add(val)
                cols[c].add(val)
                boxes[box_index(r, c)].add(val)

    def backtrack(index):
        if index == len(empty):
            return True
        r, c = empty[index]
        b = box_index(r, c)
        for digit in '123456789':
            if digit not in rows[r] and digit not in cols[c] and digit not in boxes[b]:
                board[r][c] = digit
                rows[r].add(digit)
                cols[c].add(digit)
                boxes[b].add(digit)
                if backtrack(index + 1):
                    return True
                rows[r].remove(digit)
                cols[c].remove(digit)
                boxes[b].remove(digit)
                board[r][c] = '.'
        return False

    backtrack(0)
    return board

approaches.name: Backtracking with Bitmask State
approaches.idea: Encode the digits used in every row, column, and box as bits of an integer. A digit is legal when (rows[r] | cols[c] | boxes[b]) has that bit clear; set and clear bits as the search places and retracts digits. Bitwise tests make the constraints compact and fast.
approaches.python:
def solve_sudoku_bits(board):
    rows = [0] * 9
    cols = [0] * 9
    boxes = [0] * 9
    empty = []

    def box_index(r, c):
        return (r // 3) * 3 + c // 3

    for r in range(9):
        for c in range(9):
            ch = board[r][c]
            if ch == '.':
                empty.append((r, c))
            else:
                bit = 1 << int(ch)
                rows[r] |= bit
                cols[c] |= bit
                boxes[box_index(r, c)] |= bit

    def backtrack(index):
        if index == len(empty):
            return True
        r, c = empty[index]
        b = box_index(r, c)
        used = rows[r] | cols[c] | boxes[b]
        for digit in range(1, 10):
            bit = 1 << digit
            if used & bit:
                continue
            board[r][c] = str(digit)
            rows[r] |= bit
            cols[c] |= bit
            boxes[b] |= bit
            if backtrack(index + 1):
                return True
            rows[r] ^= bit
            cols[c] ^= bit
            boxes[b] ^= bit
            board[r][c] = '.'
        return False

    backtrack(0)
    return board

approaches.name: Backtracking with MRV Heuristic
approaches.idea: Instead of filling cells in order, always pick the empty cell with the fewest legal candidates (minimum remaining values) and branch only over those. Dead ends are detected early by recomputing candidates from the row/column/box sets, pruning the search tree aggressively.
approaches.python:
def solve_sudoku_mrv(board):
    rows = [set() for _ in range(9)]
    cols = [set() for _ in range(9)]
    boxes = [set() for _ in range(9)]

    def box_index(r, c):
        return (r // 3) * 3 + c // 3

    for r in range(9):
        for c in range(9):
            val = board[r][c]
            if val != '.':
                rows[r].add(val)
                cols[c].add(val)
                boxes[box_index(r, c)].add(val)

    def candidates(r, c):
        return [d for d in '123456789'
                if d not in rows[r] and d not in cols[c] and d not in boxes[box_index(r, c)]]

    def solve():
        best_r = best_c = -1
        best_cands = None
        for r in range(9):
            for c in range(9):
                if board[r][c] == '.':
                    cands = candidates(r, c)
                    if not cands:
                        return False

            cols[best_c].remove(digit)
            boxes[b].remove(digit)
            board[best_r][best_c] = '.'
        return False

    solve()
    return board
