approaches.name: Memoized Recursion (Top-Down DP)
approaches.idea: Define dp(i, j) as whether s[i:] matches p[j:]. A '*' either consumes one character or nothing, while '?' or a literal must equal the current character. Memoizing the (i, j) states collapses the exponential search into a polynomial number of distinct subproblems.

approaches.name: Bottom-Up 2D Dynamic Programming
approaches.idea: Fill a table dp[i][j] meaning s[:i] matches p[:j]. Rows seed the base case where '*' can match an empty prefix, then each cell follows the recurrences: '*' combines skip-or-consume, and '?' or literals require a one-character match.

approaches.name: Two-Pointer Greedy with Star Backtracking
approaches.idea: Scan with two pointers while remembering the last '*' seen and the text position it consumed. When a later mismatch happens, backtrack by letting that star consume one more character. Linear memory and typically linear time, with an O(m*n) worst case only for many stars.

approaches.name: BFS Level-Order Traversal
approaches.idea: Process the tree level by level with a queue. At each level, the last node removed from the queue is the rightmost node, so its value is appended to the result.

approaches.name: DFS Right-First Recursion
approaches.idea: Pre-order traversal that explores the right child before the left child. The first node reached at any given depth is the rightmost node, so its value is recorded exactly when depth equals the length of the result built so far.

approaches.name: Iterative DFS with Explicit Stack
approaches.idea: Replace recursion with an explicit stack of (node, depth) pairs. Pushing the left child before the right child makes the right subtree pop first, so the first recorded value at each depth is again the rightmost node.

animation.hint: Notice that each horizontal level contributes exactly its rightmost node to the answer.

approaches.name: O(1) Frequency Buckets + minFreq
approaches.idea: Keep value and frequency maps plus a bucket map from frequency to an insertion-ordered set of keys. Track minFreq so eviction removes the least-frequently-used key, breaking ties by least recently used, all in constant time per operation.

approaches.name: Min-Heap of (freq, seq, key)
approaches.idea: Push the entry (freq, access-sequence, key) onto a min-heap on every access and lazily discard stale entries whose stored frequency no longer matches the live map. The heap orders by frequency then recency, so its valid top is the exact eviction candidate.
approaches.python:
import heapq

class LFUCacheHeap:
    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self.capacity = capacity
        self.cache = {}
        self.freqs = {}
        self.heap = []
        self.tick = 0

    def _bump(self, key):
        self.tick += 1
        self.freqs[key] += 1
        heapq.heappush(self.heap, (self.freqs[key], self.tick, key))

    def get(self, key):
        if key not in self.cache:
            return -1
        self._bump(key)
        return self.cache[key]

    def put(self, key, value):
        if self.capacity <= 0:
            return
        if key in self.cache:
            self.cache[key] = value
            self._bump(key)
            return
        if len(self.cache) >= self.capacity:
            self._evict()
        self.cache[key] = value
        self.freqs[key] = 1
        self.tick += 1
        heapq.heappush(self.heap, (1, self.tick, key))

    def _evict(self):
        while True:
            freq, _, key = heapq.heappop(self.heap)
            if key in self.cache and self.freqs[key] == freq:
                del self.cache[key]
                del self.freqs[key]
                return

approaches.idea: Store each entry as a flat record (key, value, freq, last-use sequence). Every operation scans the list, and eviction selects the entry with the smallest (freq, last-use) pair. The simplest possible structure, traded for linear time per operation.

class LFUCacheLinear:
    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self.capacity = capacity
        self.entries = []
        self.tick = 0

    def get(self, key):
        for entry in self.entries:
            if entry[0] == key:
                entry[2] += 1
                entry[3] = self.tick
                self.tick += 1
                return entry[1]
        return -1

    def put(self, key, value):
        if self.capacity <= 0:
            return
        for entry in self.entries:
            if entry[0] == key:
                entry[1] = value
                entry[2] += 1
                entry[3] = self.tick
                self.tick += 1
                return
        if len(self.entries) >= self.capacity:
            victim = min(self.entries, key=lambda e: (e[2], e[3]))
            self.entries.remove(victim)
        self.entries.append([key, value, 1, self.tick])
        self.tick += 1

approaches.name: Row Simulation with Direction Flip
approaches.idea: Walk the input once while bouncing a current-row index between 0 and numRows-1, appending each character to that row's buffer. The direction flips whenever the index hits the top or bottom row, then the buffers are concatenated.

approaches.name: Period-Based Row Assignment
approaches.idea: Characters repeat every period p = 2*numRows-2 positions. For index i, the row is min(i % p, p - i % p), computed in closed form and appended directly to the right buffer without tracking any movement state.

approaches.name: Direct Index Math Row by Row
approaches.idea: Build the output one row at a time and compute character positions directly: vertical columns start at row r and step by the period, while each inner row also contributes one diagonal character at period-r per cycle. No traversal or bookkeeping needed.

animation.hint: Watch characters bounce between row buffers as the direction flips at the top and bottom rows.

approaches.name: Binary Search over Integers
approaches.idea: Search the range 0..x/2 for the largest integer whose square is at most x. Comparing mid*mid against x narrows the interval in half each round until the low and high pointers converge on floor(sqrt(x)).

approaches.name: Newton-Raphson Iteration
approaches.idea: Apply the Newton iteration guess = (guess + x / guess) / 2 starting from x. The sequence converges quadratically to sqrt(x); stop as soon as guess*guess no longer exceeds x, which is exactly floor(sqrt(x)) for integers.

approaches.name: Bit-by-Bit Construction
approaches.idea: Assemble the answer from the most significant bit down. Tentatively add each power-of-four bit and keep it only if the resulting candidate squared still fits in x, producing floor(sqrt(x)) one binary digit at a time.

animation.hint: Watch the low and high pointers squeeze together to find the largest integer whose square still fits in x.

approaches.name: Two-Pointer Race
approaches.idea: Walk two pointers at identical speed; whenever one reaches the end, redirect it to the other list's head. After one full pass both pointers are aligned with respect to the shared tail and they meet exactly at the intersection node.

approaches.name: Length Alignment
approaches.idea: Measure both lists, advance the head of the longer list so both pointers are equally far from the end, then walk in lockstep. Since the lists now have equal remaining length, the first equal node is the intersection.

approaches.name: Hash Set of Visited Nodes
approaches.idea: Insert every node object of the first list into a hash set, then walk the second list and return the first node found in the set. Relies on object identity, so sharing the tail is detected immediately.

animation.hint: Both pointers travel the same total distance and converge on the shared node.

approaches.name: Top-Down Memoization + Binary Search
approaches.idea: Sort jobs by start time and define dp(i) as the best profit using jobs i..n-1. Each job is either skipped or taken, in which case its profit is added to dp of the first job whose start is at least this job's end, located by binary search.

approaches.name: Bottom-Up DP Sorted by End Time
approaches.idea: Sort jobs by end time and fill dp[i+1] = max(dp[i], profit + dp[j]) where j is the count of jobs that finish by the current job's start. The prefix dp array holds the best profit for every completion time, and binary search finds j.
approaches.python:
import bisect

def job_scheduling_dp(start_time, end_time, profit):
    jobs = sorted(zip(end_time, start_time, profit))
    ends = [job[0] for job in jobs]
    n = len(jobs)
    dp = [0] * (n + 1)
    for i in range(n):
        end, start, p = jobs[i]
        prev = bisect.bisect_right(ends, start)
        dp[i + 1] = max(dp[i], p + dp[prev])
    return dp[n]

approaches.name: Time-Coordinate Sweep
approaches.idea: Compress all start and end times into sorted indices and sweep them left to right, keeping best[i] = the maximum profit schedulable up to that time as a running prefix. Each job ending at time e proposes best[start] + profit, so the answer is the final prefix maximum.

approaches.name: Kadane-Style Min/Max Tracking
approaches.idea: Walk the array keeping both curMax and curMin at each position because multiplying by a negative flips the sign. The best answer is the largest curMax seen, and the min/max pairs are updated from x, curMax*x, and curMin*x together.

def max_product(nums):
    best = nums[0]
    cur_max = cur_min = nums[0]
    for x in nums[1:]:
        candidates = (x, cur_max * x, cur_min * x)
        cur_max, cur_min = max(candidates), min(candidates)
        best = max(best, cur_max)
    return best

approaches.name: Forward and Backward Product Sweeps
approaches.idea: Compute prefix products left-to-right and suffix products right-to-left, resetting to 1 whenever a zero is seen, and keep the maximum. Any subarray that realizes the max product is covered by one of the two directional sweeps, so the max of both passes is the answer.

approaches.name: Brute-Force Subarray Enumeration
approaches.idea: Enumerate every subarray with nested loops: for each start, extend the end one step at a time while accumulating the running product and refreshing the best value. Straightforward and correct, but quadratic because every subarray is considered.

approaches.name: Iterative Row Building
approaches.idea: Each row is built from the previous row: pad the previous row with zeros on both ends, then each new value is the sum of two adjacent padded values. The endpoints naturally become 1 and every cell is computed exactly once.

def generate(num_rows):

approaches.idea: The k-th entry of row n is the binomial coefficient C(n, k). Each row is generated in place with the recurrence C(n, k) = C(n, k-1) * (n-k+1) / k, so no previous row is needed at all.

approaches.name: Recursive Memoization
approaches.idea: Compute every value from the identity C(r, c) = C(r-1, c-1) + C(r-1, c) with base cases on the edges. A memo table caches overlapping subproblems, so each cell of the triangle is evaluated only once.

approaches.name: BFS with Queue
approaches.idea: Process the tree breadth-first with a queue. Before draining the queue, record its current size: that exact number of nodes belongs to one level, so popping them yields a full level in left-to-right order.

approaches.name: Recursive DFS by Depth
approaches.idea: Traverse the tree with a pre-order recursion that carries the current depth. The first node seen at a new depth creates the next level list, and every node is appended to the list matching its depth.

approaches.name: Iterative DFS with Stack
approaches.idea: Use an explicit stack of (node, depth) pairs. Pushing the right child before the left child keeps the in-level order left to right even though nodes are processed depth-first.

animation.hint: Watch the queue: each loop iteration drains exactly one full level of the tree.

approaches.name: Stack of Indices
approaches.idea: Push the index of every unmatched '(' (starting with a -1 sentinel). On a ')' pop the top and measure the span as the distance to the new stack top; if the stack empties, push the current index as a new base.

approaches.name: Two-Pointer Counters
approaches.idea: Count '(' and ')' while scanning left to right, resetting both counters whenever ')' exceeds '(', updating the answer whenever they are equal. The scan is repeated right to left with the roles swapped to catch substrings that start with ')'.

approaches.name: Dynamic Programming
approaches.idea: Let dp[i] be the length of the longest valid substring ending at index i. A ')' either closes a direct pair with its neighbor or wraps a previously matched block, so each dp value extends from earlier dp values in O(1).

animation.hint: Watch the stack of indices: the gap between a popped index and the new top is a valid span.

approaches.name: Hash Set
approaches.idea: Insert every number into a set and return True the moment an already-seen value is encountered. Every lookup and insertion is O(1) on average.

approaches.name: Sort and Compare Adjacent
approaches.idea: Sort the array in place so any duplicates become neighbors, then scan once comparing each element with its predecessor.

approaches.name: Brute Force Pairs
approaches.idea: Check every unordered pair of indices with nested loops and return True when any two values are equal. No extra storage is used.

approaches.name: Two Pointers
approaches.idea: Place one pointer at each end and swap the characters, moving the pointers toward the center until they cross. The reversal happens in place using only a temporary variable.

def reverse_string(chars):
    left, right = 0, len(chars) - 1
    while left < right:
        chars[left], chars[right] = chars[right], chars[left]
        left += 1
        right -= 1
    return chars

approaches.idea: Swap the first and last characters, then recursively reverse the substring between them. The recursion bottoms out when the pointers meet or cross.

approaches.name: Stack
approaches.idea: Push every character onto a stack, then pop them off one by one into a new list. Because a stack is LIFO, the popped sequence is exactly the reversed input.

approaches.name: Separate Chaining
approaches.idea: Keep an array of buckets where each bucket is a singly linked list of key/value nodes selected by key % capacity. put/get/remove traverse only the one bucket a key hashes to, and duplicate keys update in place.

approaches.name: Open Addressing (Linear Probing)
approaches.idea: Store keys and values in two parallel arrays. Collisions are resolved by probing the next free slot, and deletions leave a tombstone so probe chains stay intact.

class MyHashMap:
    EMPTY = -1
    DELETED = -2

    def __init__(self):
        self.capacity = 16
        self.keys = [self.EMPTY] * self.capacity
        self.values = [0] * self.capacity

    def _hash(self, key):
        return key % self.capacity

    def put(self, key, value):
        idx = self._hash(key)
        first_deleted = None
        while self.keys[idx] != self.EMPTY:
            if self.keys[idx] == key:
                self.values[idx] = value
                return
            if self.keys[idx] == self.DELETED and first_deleted is None:
                first_deleted = idx
            idx = (idx + 1) % self.capacity
        target = first_deleted if first_deleted is not None else idx
        self.keys[target] = key
        self.values[target] = value

    def get(self, key):
        idx = self._hash(key)
        while self.keys[idx] != self.EMPTY:
            if self.keys[idx] == key:
                return self.values[idx]
            idx = (idx + 1) % self.capacity
        return -1

    def remove(self, key):
        idx = self._hash(key)
        while self.keys[idx] != self.EMPTY:
            if self.keys[idx] == key:
                self.keys[idx] = self.DELETED
                return
            idx = (idx + 1) % self.capacity

title: First Unique Character in a String

approaches.name: Two-Pass Frequency Map
approaches.idea: First pass counts how often every character appears; second pass walks the string left to right and returns the first index whose character has count exactly one.

approaches.name: Single Pass with First Index
approaches.idea: One pass stores per character both its frequency and the index where it was first seen. A final scan over the map picks the smallest first-index among characters with frequency one.

approaches.name: Brute Force Count
approaches.idea: For each position, count how many times that character occurs in the whole string; the first position whose character occurs exactly once is the answer. Uses no extra storage.

approaches.name: Staircase from Top-Right
approaches.idea: Start at the top-right corner where the value is the row maximum and the column minimum. Move left when the current value is too big and down when it is too small, so the search path only ever shrinks the search region.

approaches.name: Binary Search per Row
approaches.idea: Every row is sorted independently, so binary-search each row for the target. Rejecting impossible rows up front keeps the practical work small.

approaches.name: Divide and Conquer
approaches.idea: Split the submatrix at its middle row and column. Comparing the pivot with the target prunes the opposite quadrant, and the search recurses into the two regions that could still contain the target.
approaches.time: O((m + n) * log(m + n)) worst case

approaches.name: Reverse Second Half
approaches.idea: Find the middle node with the slow/fast pointer trick, reverse the second half of the list, then walk both halves together comparing values. Uses O(1) extra space beyond the list itself.

class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = next

def is_palindrome(head):
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
    prev = None
    while slow:
        nxt = slow.next
        slow.next = prev
        prev = slow
        slow = nxt
    left, right = head, prev
    while right:
        if left.val != right.val:
            return False
        left = left.next
        right = right.next
    return True

approaches.idea: Copy all node values into a list, then compare the list against its reverse with two pointers meeting in the middle. Random access makes the comparison trivial.

approaches.name: Recursive Pointer Trick
approaches.idea: Recurse to the tail, and as the call stack unwinds compare each tail node with a front pointer that advances one step per return. The list is never modified.

approaches.name: Greedy Single Pass
approaches.idea: Track the total net gain and a running tank. Whenever the tank drops below zero, no earlier station can be a valid start, so the candidate start jumps to the next station. If the total is non-negative the last candidate is the answer.
approaches.python:
def can_complete_circuit(gas, cost):
    total = 0
    tank = 0
    start = 0
    for i in range(len(gas)):
        total += gas[i] - cost[i]
        tank += gas[i] - cost[i]
        if tank < 0:
            tank = 0
            start = i + 1
    return start if total >= 0 else -1

approaches.idea: Try every station as the starting point and simulate a full lap, accumulating gas minus cost and aborting as soon as the tank goes negative. The first station that completes the circle is the answer.

approaches.name: Minimum Prefix Index
approaches.idea: Compute the cumulative net gain station by station and remember where its running sum is smallest. The station immediately after that minimum prefix is the unique rotation that keeps every partial sum non-negative.
approaches.python:
def can_complete_circuit(gas, cost):
    total = 0
    prefix = 0
    min_prefix = float('inf')
    answer = 0
    for i in range(len(gas)):
        total += gas[i] - cost[i]
        prefix += gas[i] - cost[i]
        if prefix < min_prefix:
            min_prefix = prefix
            answer = (i + 1) % len(gas)
    return answer if total >= 0 else -1

title: Binary Tree Zigzag Level Order Traversal

approaches.name: BFS with level reversal
approaches.idea: Traverse the tree level by level with a queue, collecting node values for each depth. After finishing a level, reverse its value list whenever the current direction is right-to-left. The direction toggles after every level.

approaches.name: DFS by depth then flip odd levels
approaches.idea: Preorder DFS records every node into a list indexed by depth, so natural left-to-right order per level is preserved. Afterwards a single sweep reverses every odd-indexed level to obtain the zigzag pattern.

approaches.name: Two-stack alternating expansion
approaches.idea: Keep two stacks that swap roles each level. While emptying the current stack you push children onto the other one, pushing left-then-right or right-then-left depending on the target direction so the next level pops out reversed automatically.

animation.hint: Watch how the level order flips direction on each level of the tree.

approaches.name: Backtracking with sets
approaches.idea: Place queens row by row, tracking attacked columns, and both diagonals using hash sets keyed by row-minus-column and row-plus-column. If a square is attacked, skip it; otherwise place the queen and recurse, undoing on the way back.
approaches.python:
def solve_n_queens(n):
    solutions = []
    board = [["."] * n for _ in range(n)]
    cols = set()
    diag1 = set()
    diag2 = set()

    def place(row):
        if row == n:
            solutions.append(["".join(r) for r in board])
            return
        for col in range(n):
            if col in cols or (row - col) in diag1 or (row + col) in diag2:
                continue
            board[row][col] = "Q"
            cols.add(col)
            diag1.add(row - col)
            diag2.add(row + col)
            place(row + 1)
            board[row][col] = "."
            cols.remove(col)
            diag1.remove(row - col)
            diag2.remove(row + col)

    place(0)
    return solutions


for solution in solve_n_queens(4):
    for line in solution:
        print(line)
    print()

approaches.idea: The same row-by-row search, but attack tracking uses plain boolean arrays: one per column, one per each of the 2n-1 anti-diagonals (index row-col+n-1), and one per diagonal (index row+col). Array lookups make the safety check O(1) and faster than hash sets.

approaches.idea: Encode attacked columns and both diagonals as single integers, one bit per column. A bitwise AND of the three masks yields the free columns, and the lowest set bit is extracted and cleared with bit tricks. This tracks the whole board state in three ints.

def solve_n_queens(n):
    solutions = []

    def backtrack(row, cols, diag1, diag2, queens):
        if row == n:
            board = []
            for r in range(n):
                line = ["."] * n
                line[queens[r]] = "Q"
                board.append("".join(line))
            solutions.append(board)
            return
        available = ((1 << n) - 1) & ~(cols | diag1 | diag2)
        while available:
            bit = available & -available
            available -= bit
            col = bit.bit_length() - 1
            queens.append(col)
            backtrack(row + 1, cols | bit, (diag1 | bit) << 1, (diag2 | bit) >> 1, queens)
            queens.pop()

    backtrack(0, 0, 0, 0, [])
    return solutions


for solution in solve_n_queens(4):
    for line in solution:
        print(line)
    print()

approaches.name: Sum formula
approaches.idea: The integers from 0 to n sum to n*(n+1)/2. Subtract the actual sum of the array from that closed-form total and the difference is exactly the missing value.

approaches.name: XOR cancellation
approaches.idea: XOR every index together with every array value. Each value from 0 to n appears twice except the missing one, and because x XOR x cancels to 0, only the missing number remains in the accumulated result.

approaches.name: Sort and scan
approaches.idea: Sort the array so every element should equal its own index. Walk through the sorted array and return the first index where value and index diverge; if none diverge, the missing value is n itself.

animation.hint: Each value that appears twice cancels out, leaving only the missing number.

approaches.name: Binary search over flattened index
approaches.idea: Because rows are sorted and each row starts after the previous row ends, the matrix behaves like one sorted array of size rows*cols. A single binary search maps the mid index back to (row, col) using division and modulo.

approaches.name: Two-step binary search
approaches.idea: First binary search down the first column to find the last row whose first element is no larger than the target. Then run a normal binary search inside that single row. Each phase halves a different dimension.

approaches.name: Staircase walk from top-right
approaches.idea: Start at the top-right corner. If the current cell is larger than the target, move left; if smaller, move down; if equal, you are done. Because rows and columns are sorted this walk never revisits a cell and exits when it falls off the matrix.

animation.hint: The flattened binary search maps a linear mid index back to its matrix cell.

approaches.name: Running left sum
approaches.idea: Compute the total sum once, then walk the array keeping a running left sum. At each index the right-hand sum equals total minus left-sum minus the current element, so compare left and right and return the first index where they match.

approaches.name: Prefix sum arrays
approaches.idea: Build a prefix array where prefix[i] holds the sum of everything before index i. Then the left side of i is prefix[i] and the right side is total minus prefix[i+1]. Scanning i and comparing these two precomputed sums finds the pivot directly.

approaches.name: Brute force per index
approaches.idea: For every candidate index compute the sums of the elements strictly to its left and strictly to its right from scratch. Whichever index has equal sides is the pivot. This is the naive baseline that recomputes sums repeatedly.

animation.hint: The pivot is where the running left sum equals total minus left sum minus the pivot value.

approaches.name: Max-frequency formula
approaches.idea: Only the most frequent task matters for the framework of the schedule. The total time is the length of the tasks, or (maxCount-1)*(n+1) plus the number of tasks sharing that max count, whichever is larger. No simulation is needed.

approaches.name: Max-heap with cooldown queue
approaches.idea: Simulate time unit by unit. A max-heap holds the tasks ready to run, and a FIFO cooldown queue stores (readyTime, count) pairs for tasks waiting out their cooldown. Each tick releases tasks whose cooldown expired and runs the most frequent ready task, or idles.

approaches.name: Greedy slot simulation
approaches.idea: Walk through time and at each unit pick the available task type with the largest remaining count by a linear scan over the 26 frequency buckets. A cooldown array records when each type becomes schedulable again; if nothing is available, the unit is idle.

animation.hint: Each time unit either schedules the most frequent ready task or ticks idle while everything cools down.

approaches.name: BFS with visited map
approaches.idea: Use a queue to walk the original graph while a hash map links each original node to its fresh copy. When visiting a neighbor for the first time a copy is made and enqueued; every neighbor copy is wired into the current copy's adjacency list.

approaches.name: Recursive DFS with visited map
approaches.idea: A recursive function clones a node by first returning the cached copy when it already exists. Otherwise it creates the copy, stores it in the map before recursing, and appends the clones of all neighbors, which handles cycles naturally.

approaches.name: Iterative DFS with visited map
approaches.idea: Replace the recursion with an explicit stack. Each node is copied and registered the first time it is seen, pushed onto the stack, and popped to connect its clone to the clones of all neighbors. Same structure as BFS but uses depth-first exploration order.

animation.hint: Each original node is paired with its copy in a map before its neighbors are cloned.

approaches.name: Position product array
approaches.idea: The product of digit at position i of num1 and position j of num2 lands at positions i+j and i+j+1 of a length n+m accumulator. Fill the array with all digit products, propagate carries, and drop leading zeros to build the result.

approaches.name: Partial products with string addition
approaches.idea: Mimic manual long multiplication: multiply each digit of num1 against the whole of num2, producing a shifted partial product, then add every partial product into a running string sum using a digit-by-digit addition helper.
approaches.python:
def multiply_strings(num1, num2):
    if num1 == "0" or num2 == "0":
        return "0"

    def add(x, y):
        i, j = len(x) - 1, len(y) - 1
        carry = 0
        result = []
        while i >= 0 or j >= 0 or carry:
            d1 = int(x[i]) if i >= 0 else 0
            d2 = int(y[j]) if j >= 0 else 0
            total = d1 + d2 + carry
            result.append(str(total % 10))
            carry = total // 10
            i -= 1
            j -= 1
        return "".join(reversed(result))

    result = "0"
    trailing = 0
    for i in range(len(num1) - 1, -1, -1):
        carry = 0
        partial = []
        for j in range(len(num2) - 1, -1, -1):
            total = int(num1[i]) * int(num2[j]) + carry
            partial.append(str(total % 10))
            carry = total // 10
        if carry:
            partial.append(str(carry))
        partial = "".join(reversed(partial)) + "0" * trailing
        result = add(result, partial)
        trailing += 1
    return result


print(multiply_strings("123", "456"))

approaches.name: Karatsuba divide and conquer
approaches.idea: Split both factors into high and low halves around m digits. Compute three recursive products z0=low*low, z1=(low+high)*(low+high), z2=high*high, then reconstruct z2*10^(2m) + (z1-z0-z2)*10^m + z0 using pure string arithmetic helpers for add and subtract.

animation.hint: Digit products accumulate into fixed positions and carries ripple toward the front.

approaches.name: Memoized DFS
approaches.idea: A recursive function over the start index tries every substring that is a dictionary word and recurses on the remainder. Results for each start index are cached so repeated subproblems never recompute their sentence lists.

approaches.name: Bottom-up dynamic programming
approaches.idea: Build sentence lists forward: dp[i] holds all sentences for the prefix of length i. For every cut j before i whose substring s[j:i] is a word, append that word to every sentence already in dp[j] and store them in dp[i].

approaches.name: Trie-powered backtracking
approaches.idea: Insert all dictionary words into a trie. DFS walks the string character by character through the trie; whenever the current trie node marks a word end, take that substring as a segment and continue the walk from the next position, collecting every complete segmentation.

animation.hint: Sentences for shorter prefixes are built first and extended by each matching dictionary word.

approaches.name: Sieve of Eratosthenes
approaches.idea: Start with all numbers 0..n-1 marked prime, then iterate from 2 up to sqrt(n) and mark every multiple of each prime as composite. The remaining marked entries are exactly the primes below n.

approaches.name: Odd-only sieve
approaches.idea: A refined sieve that first clears every even number, then only scans odd candidates starting from 3 and marks odd multiples with a step of 2*i. This roughly halves both the marking work and the storage touched.

approaches.name: Trial division with 6k+-1
approaches.idea: Check each candidate below n individually. Any prime above 3 lives in the form 6k-1 or 6k+1, so after ruling out divisibility by 2 and 3, only divisors of that form up to the square root need testing.

animation.hint: Multiples of each discovered prime flip from prime to composite until only primes remain.

approaches.name: Recursive Mirror Check
approaches.idea: A binary tree is symmetric if its left and right subtrees are mirror images of each other. A recursive helper compares two nodes at a time: they must be equal, and the outer children and inner children must mirror each other in turn. This is the cleanest formulation of the problem.

approaches.name: Iterative Queue (BFS)
approaches.idea: Use a queue to compare nodes in pairs, mirroring the recursive idea without recursion. Pop two nodes at a time and verify they match; then push their mirror pairs (left-right and right-left) for later inspection. If any mismatched pair is found, the tree is not symmetric.

approaches.name: Iterative Stack (DFS)
approaches.idea: The same pair-comparison strategy can be driven by an explicit stack instead of a queue, making the traversal depth-first. Push mirror pairs onto the stack and pop them one by one, returning false on the first mismatch. This avoids recursion entirely while keeping identical logic.

animation.hint: Compare the left and right subtrees as mirror images, always pairing outer with outer and inner with inner.

approaches.name: Max-Heap Greedy
approaches.idea: Count every character and push (count, char) into a max-heap. Repeatedly pop the most frequent remaining character, append it, and hold it aside for one step so the same character is never placed twice in a row. If the final held count is still positive the string cannot be reorganized.

approaches.name: Even/Odd Slot Filling
approaches.idea: The most frequent character limits the answer, so check that no count exceeds (n + 1) / 2. Then order all characters by decreasing frequency and pour them into the output array at even indices first and odd indices after, which automatically separates any equal characters.

approaches.name: Frequency-Array Linear Greedy
approaches.idea: Keep a 26-entry frequency table and build the answer position by position. At every step scan the table and pick the most frequent character that is not the one just placed, then decrement it. The O(26n) scan replaces a heap and is easy to trace step by step.

animation.hint: Always place the most frequent character next, but never the character that was just placed.

approaches.name: Recursive Post-Order Height
approaches.idea: The diameter is the longest path between any two nodes, which always passes through some node and equals the sum of the heights of its two subtrees. A recursive function computes each subtree's height while a global maximum tracks the best left+right sum seen so far.

approaches.name: Iterative Post-Order with State Stack
approaches.idea: Emulate the recursive post-order traversal with an explicit stack holding (node, visited) pairs. On the second visit the subtree heights are known, so the code computes height and updates the diameter without recursion. This works on trees deep enough to overflow the call stack.

approaches.name: Double BFS Farthest Node
approaches.idea: A classic graph fact: the diameter of a tree equals the distance between its two farthest nodes. Record parent pointers, run one BFS from an arbitrary root to find the farthest node A, then run a second BFS from A; the maximum distance reached is exactly the diameter. No height bookkeeping is needed.

animation.hint: The diameter passes through some node and equals the sum of its two subtree heights.

approaches.name: Sort + Two Pointers
approaches.idea: Sort the array, then fix the first two elements with nested loops and sweep the remaining two with a left/right pointer pair. When the total is too small move the left pointer, when too large move the right, and skip duplicate values to keep the answer unique.

approaches.name: Pair-Sum Hash Map
approaches.idea: Record every pair sum together with the two indices that produced it in a hash map. Then for every other pair, look up the complementary sum and accept the quadruple only when the indices are strictly ordered. A set removes duplicates caused by equal values.

approaches.name: Recursive K-Sum Reduction
approaches.idea: Generalize the problem to k-sum: to find k numbers with a given sum, fix one candidate and recurse on k-1 with the reduced target. The base case k=2 is solved with the two-pointer sweep on the sorted array, and duplicate values are skipped at every level.

animation.hint: Sort first, fix the first two numbers, then shrink two pointers from both ends.

approaches.name: Monotonic Stack
approaches.idea: Scan the digits left to right and maintain a stack that stays increasing from bottom to top. Whenever the next digit is smaller than the top of the stack, pop the top because removing that larger digit makes the number smaller. After the scan, trim any leftover removals and strip leading zeros.

approaches.name: Repeated Single-Pass Removal
approaches.idea: Removing one digit at a time: scan the number until the first place where a digit is greater than its successor, delete that digit, and repeat k times. Deleting the first 'descent' is always optimal for one removal, so repeating the greedy choice yields the best result.

approaches.name: Greedy Window Selection
approaches.idea: Think of it as keeping exactly len(num) - k digits. For each kept position, scan a window of still-eligible digits and pick the minimum, then continue from just after it. Choosing the smallest digit in each window is provably optimal and skips the deleted digits without mutating the string.

animation.hint: Keep the stack strictly increasing so the biggest early digits get removed first.

approaches.name: Conditional Branching
approaches.idea: Loop over the numbers and branch on the classic rules in the right order. Checking divisibility by 15 first catches FizzBuzz, then Fizz for multiples of 3 and Buzz for multiples of 5, otherwise output the number itself. Simple, direct, and matches the statement literally.

approaches.name: Additive String Concatenation
approaches.idea: Instead of if/else chains, append the matching words with independent checks and only fall back to the number when nothing was appended. The two conditions compose naturally: a multiple of 15 gets both 'Fizz' and 'Buzz', producing 'FizzBuzz' without a special 15 case.

approaches.name: Rule Table Lookup
approaches.idea: Model the rules as a small table mapping divisors to words, then for each number concatenate the words of every divisor that divides it. This decouples the logic from the specific divisors, so adding a rule for 7 is just one more table entry instead of another branch.

animation.hint: Multiples of 15 satisfy both the 3 and 5 rules, producing the combined word.

approaches.name: Floyd's Cycle Detection
approaches.idea: Treat the array as a linked list where index i points to nums[i]; because a value repeats, this functional graph contains a cycle. The tortoise and hare meet inside the cycle, and resetting the tortoise to the start then moving both one step at a time finds the cycle entry, which is the duplicate.

approaches.name: Binary Search on Value Range
approaches.idea: The duplicate value lies between 1 and n, so binary search the answer over that value range. Count how many numbers are at most the midpoint; if the count exceeds the midpoint, the duplicate must be in the lower half, otherwise it is in the upper half. No array mutation is needed.

approaches.name: In-Place Negative Marking
approaches.idea: Walk through the array and mark each visited value's target index by negating it. If we ever step onto an already-negative cell, that index is the duplicate. This runs in linear time and constant extra space, at the cost of modifying the input array.

animation.hint: Follow nums[i] as the next index and detect the repeated entry.

title: All Nodes Distance K in Binary Tree

approaches.name: Parent Pointers + BFS
approaches.idea: Tree edges only go downward, so record each node's parent with a DFS to turn the tree into an undirected graph. Then start a BFS from the target node, moving to children and parents, and collect every node reached at distance exactly k. BFS guarantees nodes are visited by increasing distance.

approaches.name: Undirected Graph + DFS
approaches.idea: Build an explicit adjacency list where every parent-child edge is stored in both directions, then run a depth-first search from the target counting steps. The visited set prevents walking back over already-visited nodes, and nodes hit at exactly distance k are recorded. DFS explores the same reachable set as BFS but with a different traversal order.

approaches.name: Recursive Distance Propagation
approaches.idea: Solve the problem without building any graph. First find the target in the tree, returning its depth along the way; from each ancestor, the target lies in one subtree, so all qualifying nodes live in the other subtree at a computable distance. Nodes at distance k inside the target's own subtree are collected by a plain downward walk.

animation.hint: Follow parent and child edges outward from the target exactly k steps.

approaches.name: 2D Bottom-Up DP
approaches.idea: The minimal cost to reach a cell is its value plus the smaller of the costs to reach the cell above or the cell to its left. Fill the grid in reading order, seeding the top row and left column first, then the bottom-right cell holds the answer. This is the canonical dynamic-programming solution.

approaches.name: 1D Rolling DP
approaches.idea: Each row of the DP table only depends on the row above it, so a single array of length cols is enough. While sweeping a row, update each entry as the cell cost plus the minimum of its own previous value (from above) and the just-updated left neighbor. Space drops from O(m*n) to O(n).

approaches.name: Dijkstra Shortest Path
approaches.idea: Model the grid as a weighted directed graph where every edge has the destination cell's cost and move right or down. Run Dijkstra's algorithm from the top-left with a min-priority queue; the first time the bottom-right is popped its distance is the minimum path sum. No DP recurrence is needed.
approaches.python:
import heapq


def min_path_sum(grid):
    rows = len(grid)
    cols = len(grid[0])
    distances = [[float("inf")] * cols for _ in range(rows)]
    distances[0][0] = grid[0][0]
    heap = [(grid[0][0], 0, 0)]
    while heap:
        cost, r, c = heapq.heappop(heap)
        if r == rows - 1 and c == cols - 1:
            return cost
        for dr, dc in ((1, 0), (0, 1)):
            nr = r + dr
            nc = c + dc
            if 0 <= nr < rows and 0 <= nc < cols:
                new_cost = cost + grid[nr][nc]
                if new_cost < distances[nr][nc]:
                    distances[nr][nc] = new_cost
                    heapq.heappush(heap, (new_cost, nr, nc))
    return -1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    grid = [[1, 3, 1],
            [1, 5, 1],
            [4, 2, 1]]
    print(min_path_sum(grid))

animation.hint: Each cell's best cost is its value plus the smaller of the top and left neighbors.

approaches.name: Per-Row Histogram + Monotonic Stack
approaches.idea: Reduce each row to a histogram where height[j] counts consecutive 1s ending at this row. The problem becomes the classic largest-rectangle-in-histogram, solved with a monotonic stack in one pass per row. The largest area over all rows is the answer.

approaches.name: Left/Right Boundary DP
approaches.idea: For every cell keep three running facts: the height of 1s above it, the leftmost column the current row can extend to, and the rightmost column it can extend to. Combining right - left with height gives the widest rectangle ending at each cell, updated row by row with only three arrays.

approaches.name: Brute-Force Rectangle Expansion
approaches.idea: Try every cell as the top-left corner of a rectangle and expand downward row by row, always shrinking the width to the narrowest run of consecutive 1s found so far. Every expansion yields a candidate area, and the maximum over all top-left corners is the largest rectangle. Straightforward and mutation-free.

animation.hint: Turn each row into a histogram of consecutive 1s and find the largest rectangle per row.

approaches.name: Recursive descent parser
approaches.idea: Parses the expression with a small grammar: expr = term ((+|-) term)*, term = factor ((*|/) factor)*, factor = number or ( expr ). A single cursor walks the string, an opening parenthesis recurses into parse_expr and its closing parenthesis returns. This mirrors the arithmetic grammar directly, so precedence and parentheses need no explicit operator table.
approaches.python:
def calculate(s):
    s = s.replace(" ", "")
    i = 0
    n = len(s)

    def parse_expr():
        nonlocal i
        val = parse_term()
        while i < n and s[i] in "+-":
            op = s[i]
            i += 1
            rhs = parse_term()
            val = val + rhs if op == "+" else val - rhs
        return val

    def parse_term():
        nonlocal i
        val = parse_factor()
        while i < n and s[i] in "*/":
            op = s[i]
            i += 1
            rhs = parse_factor()
            val = val * rhs if op == "*" else int(val / rhs)
        return val

    def parse_factor():
        nonlocal i
        if s[i] == "(":
            i += 1
            val = parse_expr()
            i += 1
            return val
        start = i
        while i < n and s[i].isdigit():
            i += 1
        return int(s[start:i])

    return parse_expr()


print(calculate("2*(5+5*2)/3+(6/2+8)"))

approaches.name: Two-stack shunting-yard
approaches.idea: Evaluates the expression with an operator stack and an operand stack (shunting-yard). * and / have higher precedence, so when an operator arrives we pop and apply every operator on top whose precedence is >= the new one, before pushing it. Parentheses are handled by pushing '(' blindly and evaluating back to '(' on ')'. All + and - then run left-to-right.

approaches.name: Parenthesis-elimination recursion
approaches.idea: Tokenizes the string, then repeatedly locates the first closing parenthesis, finds the matching opening one just before it, evaluates that inner chunk with a tiny linear +-*/ evaluator, and substitutes the numeric result back into the token list. Once no parentheses remain, the flat token list is evaluated a final time.
approaches.python:
import re


def eval_simple(tokens):
    vals = [int(tokens[0])]
    ops = []
    idx = 1
    while idx < len(tokens):
        op = tokens[idx]
        num = int(tokens[idx + 1])
        if op in "*/":
            last = vals.pop()
            vals.append(last * num if op == "*" else int(last / num))
        else:
            ops.append(op)
            vals.append(num)
        idx += 2
    total = vals[0]
    for k, op in enumerate(ops):
        total = total + vals[k + 1] if op == "+" else total - vals[k + 1]
    return total


def calculate(s):
    tokens = re.findall(r"\d+|[()+\-*/]", s)
    while "(" in tokens:
        close = tokens.index(")")
        open_idx = max(i for i in range(close) if tokens[i] == "(")
        inner = eval_simple(tokens[open_idx + 1:close])
        tokens = tokens[:open_idx] + [str(inner)] + tokens[close + 1:]
    return eval_simple(tokens)


print(calculate("2*(5+5*2)/3+(6/2+8)"))

animation.hint: Watch the operator stack: an operator is applied as soon as a higher-or-equal-precedence operator arrives, and a ')' drains everything back to '('.

approaches.name: First/last/count maps
approaches.idea: A single pass records for every value its first index, its last index, and its frequency in three maps. The degree is the maximum frequency, and the answer is the smallest last-first+1 span among all values that reach that degree.

approaches.name: Sliding window
approaches.idea: First computes the global degree D with a frequency map. A two-pointer window then slides right: when the value just added reaches count D the window is valid, so its length is recorded and the window shrinks from the left while the anchor value still has count D. The minimum length ever recorded is the answer.
approaches.python:
def find_shortest_subarray(nums):
    from collections import Counter

    degree = max(Counter(nums).values())
    counts = Counter()
    left = 0
    best = len(nums)
    for right, v in enumerate(nums):
        counts[v] += 1
        while counts[v] == degree:
            best = min(best, right - left + 1)
            counts[nums[left]] -= 1
            left += 1
    return best


print(find_shortest_subarray([1, 2, 2, 3, 1]))

approaches.name: Span closure with remaining counts
approaches.idea: Counts frequencies first, then makes one forward pass that opens a span at each value's first occurrence and closes it exactly when that value's remaining count reaches zero. Any closed span whose value has the maximum frequency is a candidate; the minimum width wins.

animation.hint: count tracks how often each value appears; the answer is the shortest span that still contains the most frequent value.

approaches.name: O(1) line counters
approaches.idea: Keeps one running counter per row, per column, and for the two diagonals. Player 1 adds +1 and player 2 adds -1 to every affected line; as soon as any line reaches magnitude n the move wins. Each move costs constant time and no board is stored.
approaches.python:
class TicTacToe:
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.n = n
        self.rows = [0] * n
        self.cols = [0] * n
        self.diag = 0
        self.anti = 0

    def move(self, row, col, player):
        val = 1 if player == 1 else -1
        self.rows[row] += val
        self.cols[col] += val
        if row == col:
            self.diag += val
        if row + col == self.n - 1:
            self.anti += val
        if (abs(self.rows[row]) == self.n or abs(self.cols[col]) == self.n
                or abs(self.diag) == self.n or abs(self.anti) == self.n):
            return player
        return 0


board = TicTacToe(3)
moves = [(0, 0, 1), (0, 2, 2), (2, 2, 1), (1, 1, 2), (2, 0, 1), (0, 1, 2), (2, 1, 1)]
print([board.move(r, c, p) for r, c, p in moves])

approaches.name: Matrix with affected-line scan
approaches.idea: Stores the real n x n board. After each move it only re-checks the four lines that pass through the new mark: the move's row, its column, and the two diagonals only if the mark lies on them. This is O(n) per move but extremely easy to reason about and explain.

approaches.name: Bitmask line tracking
approaches.idea: Encodes each candidate line as an integer bitmask per player: one mask for rows, one for columns, one for each diagonal. A move ORs the appropriate bit into those masks, and a mask equal to (1<<n)-1 means that player has filled a whole line. Each move is constant time with pure bit operations.
approaches.python:
class TicTacToe:
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.n = n
        self.p1 = [0, 0, 0, 0]  # rows, cols, diag, anti
        self.p2 = [0, 0, 0, 0]

    def move(self, row, col, player):
        n = self.n
        groups = self.p1 if player == 1 else self.p2
        groups[0] |= 1 << row
        groups[1] |= 1 << col
        if row == col:
            groups[2] |= 1 << row
        if row + col == n - 1:
            groups[3] |= 1 << row
        full = (1 << n) - 1
        if full in groups:
            return player
        return 0


board = TicTacToe(3)
moves = [(0, 0, 1), (0, 2, 2), (2, 2, 1), (1, 1, 2), (2, 0, 1), (0, 1, 2), (2, 1, 1)]
print([board.move(r, c, p) for r, c, p in moves])

animation.hint: Each move places a mark; a player wins the moment one row, column, or diagonal is completely filled.

approaches.name: Recursive Hierholzer (Eulerian path)
approaches.idea: Builds an Eulerian path using post-order DFS. From JFK, always consume the lexicographically smallest unused outgoing edge; airports are appended to the route only when their edge lists are exhausted, then the route is reversed. Sorting destinations descending lets pop() yield the smallest edge first, which produces the lexicographically smallest itinerary.

approaches.name: Iterative Hierholzer with explicit stack
approaches.idea: The same Eulerian path construction, but written iteratively with an explicit stack of airports. The current top of the stack always advances to its smallest unused destination; when it has no edges left it is a dead end, so it is moved onto the route. Reversing the collected route yields the itinerary.

approaches.name: Backtracking DFS with edge restoration
approaches.idea: Explores from JFK trying destinations in lexicographic order, temporarily removing each edge as it descends. The first path that uses every ticket is returned immediately; whenever a branch dead-ends, the consumed edge is put back and the next destination is tried. Because children are always tried smallest-first, the first complete path is the answer.

animation.hint: Follow the Eulerian path: always leave an airport via its smallest unused ticket, and append the airport to the route only when all its tickets are spent.

approaches.name: Copy board and compute next state
approaches.idea: Builds a second board of the same size. Each cell's next state is decided purely from its 8 neighbors in the unchanged original board using the four classic rules, then written into the copy. Simple and clearly correct because neighbor counts never see partially updated cells.

approaches.name: In-place with two-bit encoding
approaches.idea: Encodes pending transitions inside the original cells so the old state stays readable: a live cell that dies is stored as 2 and a dead cell that becomes alive as 3. Neighbor counting treats 1 and 2 as currently alive; after the whole board is scanned, a final pass maps 2 to 0 and 3 to 1. No extra board needed.

approaches.name: Sparse pending-change updates
approaches.idea: Instead of copying the board, only the cells whose state actually changes are recorded as (row, col, newValue) triples during a full scan. The recorded changes are applied after the scan finishes, so neighbor counts always read the untouched old board while memory use is proportional to the number of changing cells.

animation.hint: Each cell's next state depends only on its 8 neighbors; encoded states let you keep the old board readable while updating in place.

approaches.name: Deduplicate then sort
approaches.idea: Treats the salary table as a list of numbers. Inserting every salary into a sorted set removes duplicates, and picking the element just below the maximum gives the second highest distinct salary. Returns null when fewer than two distinct values exist.
approaches.python:
def second_highest(salaries):
    unique = sorted(set(salaries))
    return unique[-2] if len(unique) >= 2 else None


print(second_highest([500, 300, 400, 300, 200]))

approaches.name: Two-pass maximum elimination
approaches.idea: Computes the maximum salary in one pass, then filters out every occurrence of that maximum and takes the maximum of the remainder. This works on lists with duplicates without needing any sorting. If nothing remains, there is no second distinct salary.

approaches.name: Single-pass top-two tracking
approaches.idea: Walks the list once while maintaining the largest and the second-largest distinct values seen so far. Duplicates of the current largest are skipped, so ties never corrupt the ranking. This needs no sorting and no extra copy of the data.

animation.hint: Walk the salaries once, remembering the largest and the second-largest distinct values you have seen.

approaches.name: Operand stack
approaches.idea: Scans the tokens left to right: every number is pushed onto a stack, and every operator pops the top two operands, applies the operation (truncating division toward zero), and pushes the result back. The single value left on the stack is the answer.

approaches.name: Recursion from the right
approaches.idea: In postfix form every operator is the last token of the expression it completes. Recursing from the end, an operator first evaluates the expression that produced its right operand, then the one that produced its left operand, and combines them. This mirrors the postfix tree without building it explicitly.

approaches.name: Expression tree then evaluate
approaches.idea: Parses the postfix tokens into a binary expression tree: every token becomes a node, numbers are leaves and operators become internal nodes whose right and left children are popped off a node stack. The answer is the post-order evaluation of that tree, recursively combining leaves with their operators.

animation.hint: Operands pile up; every operator pops the top two values and pushes the result back onto the stack.

approaches.name: Iterative hoisting with dummy head
approaches.idea: A dummy node guards against reversing from position 1. Walk to the node just before the segment, then repeatedly take the node after the segment start and thread it to the front of the segment. After right-left passes the whole slice is reversed and reconnects to the untouched tail.
approaches.python:
class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, nxt=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = nxt


def to_list(head):
    vals = []
    while head:
        vals.append(head.val)
        head = head.next
    return vals


def reverse_between(head, left, right):
    dummy = ListNode(0, head)
    prev = dummy
    for _ in range(left - 1):
        prev = prev.next
    start = prev.next
    current = start.next
    for _ in range(right - left):
        nxt = current.next
        current.next = prev.next
        prev.next = current
        current = nxt
    start.next = current
    return dummy.next


head = ListNode(1, ListNode(2, ListNode(3, ListNode(4, ListNode(5)))))
print(to_list(reverse_between(head, 2, 4)))

approaches.name: Array copy, slice reverse, rebuild
approaches.idea: Reads the whole list into an array, swaps the slice between the left-th and right-th positions in place, then rebuilds a fresh linked list from the array. The node structure is never touched during the reversal, which makes the transformation trivial to inspect.
approaches.python:
class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, nxt=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = nxt


def to_list(head):
    vals = []
    while head:
        vals.append(head.val)
        head = head.next
    return vals


def reverse_between(head, left, right):
    vals = []
    node = head
    while node:
        vals.append(node.val)
        node = node.next
    vals[left - 1:right] = vals[left - 1:right][::-1]
    dummy = ListNode()
    cur = dummy
    for v in vals:
        cur.next = ListNode(v)
        cur = cur.next
    return dummy.next


head = ListNode(1, ListNode(2, ListNode(3, ListNode(4, ListNode(5)))))
print(to_list(reverse_between(head, 2, 4)))

approaches.name: Stack the middle segment
approaches.idea: Walks to the node just before position left, then pushes every node of the sublist onto a stack as it walks past it. Popping the stack re-issues the nodes in reverse order, relinking them right after the saved predecessor, and finally the tail is reattached. Very easy to reason about because the reversal is done by a last-in-first-out structure.
approaches.python:
class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, nxt=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = nxt


def to_list(head):
    vals = []
    while head:
        vals.append(head.val)
        head = head.next
    return vals


def reverse_between(head, left, right):
    dummy = ListNode(0, head)
    prev = dummy
    for _ in range(left - 1):
        prev = prev.next
    stack = []
    cur = prev.next
    for _ in range(right - left + 1):
        stack.append(cur)
        cur = cur.next
    tail = cur
    while stack:
        prev.next = stack.pop()
        prev = prev.next
    prev.next = tail
    return dummy.next


head = ListNode(1, ListNode(2, ListNode(3, ListNode(4, ListNode(5)))))
print(to_list(reverse_between(head, 2, 4)))

animation.hint: Watch prev sit just before the reversed segment while each node is hoisted to the front of that segment one at a time.

title: Remove Nth Node From End of List

approaches.name: Two-pass with length
approaches.idea: First pass counts the total length of the list. A dummy head lets the second pass walk exactly length-n steps, placing a pointer at the node just before the target, whose next link is then skipped over the target.
approaches.python:
class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, nxt=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = nxt


def to_list(head):
    vals = []
    while head:
        vals.append(head.val)
        head = head.next
    return vals


def remove_nth_from_end(head, n):
    dummy = ListNode(0, head)
    length = 0
    node = head
    while node:
        length += 1
        node = node.next
    prev = dummy
    for _ in range(length - n):
        prev = prev.next
    prev.next = prev.next.next
    return dummy.next


head = ListNode(1, ListNode(2, ListNode(3, ListNode(4, ListNode(5)))))
print(to_list(remove_nth_from_end(head, 2)))

approaches.name: One-pass two-pointer gap
approaches.idea: Keeps two pointers exactly n apart: the fast pointer advances n steps first, then fast and slow move together one node at a time. When fast falls off the end, slow is precisely the node before the nth-from-end target, so its next link is skipped over.

approaches.name: Recursive count from the end
approaches.idea: A post-order recursion returns how many nodes remain below the current node. When the returned count plus one equals n, the current node is the target and its predecessor (tracked through the recursion) unlinks it. Natural depth-first bookkeeping with no length pre-computation.

animation.hint: Fast stays n steps ahead, so when fast reaches the end, slow is exactly one node before the one to delete.

approaches.name: Recursive divide and conquer
approaches.idea: The depth of a tree is 1 plus the depth of its deeper subtree, and an empty tree has depth 0. Solving the two subtrees independently and taking the maximum is the canonical recursive formulation of this problem.

approaches.name: Iterative BFS level order
approaches.idea: Processes the tree one level at a time with a queue: each complete round over the current level consumes the level and queues the next one. The number of completed rounds equals the maximum depth, since the tree is exhausted exactly after its deepest level.

approaches.name: Iterative DFS with depth stack
approaches.idea: Pushes (node, depth) pairs onto a stack, always descending into a child with depth+1 and keeping the running maximum depth. Unlike BFS this can dive to the bottom immediately, and it avoids recursion entirely.
approaches.python:
class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right


def max_depth(root):
    depth = 0
    stack = [(root, 1)]
    while stack:
        node, d = stack.pop()
        if node is None:
            continue
        depth = max(depth, d)
        stack.append((node.left, d + 1))
        stack.append((node.right, d + 1))
    return depth


root = TreeNode(3, TreeNode(9), TreeNode(20, TreeNode(15), TreeNode(7)))
print(max_depth(root))

animation.hint: Depth is 1 plus the taller subtree; the recursion bubbles the deepest level back up to the root.
